#5378. What will Social Security look like in 2027 and beyond?

Social Security recipients will get a 3.6% COLA in 2027 but also face a 2032 insolvency deadline, rising senior hardships and competing policy responses. The Senior Citizens League urges Congress to lift the payroll tax cap, restore Medicare funding and expand benefits, while a new Senate bill would instead borrow from general revenues to avoid benefit cuts, a move budget watchdogs say could add $190 trillion to federal debt over 75 years.  AI Summary

With potential program insolvency looming in 2032, the next few years for Social Security are being defined by conflicting pressures — including the 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) in 2027, quickly rising financial obstacles for older Americans, and yet another proposal in Congress that could either stabilize benefits or sharply increase federal debt levels.

Earlier this month, The Senior Citizens League forecast a 3.6% COLA for 2028, matching the Social Security Administration’s recently announced 3.6% COLA for 2027. But Morningstar noted this week that the 2027 COLA — the largest since 2023’s 8.7% adjustment — will translate into smaller take-home increases once Medicare costs are deducted.

Most Social Security beneficiaries are enrolled in Medicare Part B, and premiums are automatically deducted from monthly checks. Morningstar reported that the standard monthly Part B premium will rise by $6.50 next year to $209.40, a 3.2% increase. That will allow most beneficiaries to keep more than 3% of the 3.6% COLA after the deduction.

Morningstar calculated that a retiree receiving the average October benefit of $2,092 would see a net benefit increase of about 3.29%, assuming they pay the standard Part B premium and have no other changes in deductions. A higher-income retiree with a $3,500 monthly benefit would see a net increase of roughly 3.41% under the same assumptions.

The COLA is based on the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W), which compares the average readings for July, August and September on a year-over-year basis. Analysts cited by Morningstar noted that CPI-W may understate seniors’ actual cost pressures, particularly for healthcare, and pointed to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics’ CPI-E index for older households, which has historically risen faster than CPI-W.

The Senior Citizens League (TSCL) said the projected 3.6% COLA for 2028 is likely to arrive against a deteriorating backdrop for older adults, including senior homeowners who may still be making monthly mortgage payments. The group said that seniors are now the country’s fastest-growing homeless population and that many forgo vision, dental and hearing care due to costs.

TSCL’s release emphasized that Social Security’s primary trust fund is projected to reach insolvency in 2032, triggering automatic benefit reductions if Congress does not act. The Medicare Part A hospital insurance trust fund is projected to become insolvent in 2033, the group said.

That timing elevates the stakes for the next Congress, which will be led by Democrats after their decisive victories in the recent midterm elections. Senators elected in the current cycle will serve from Jan. 3, 2027, through Jan. 3, 2033, overlapping the projected insolvency date. TSCL framed these terms as a key window for any reforms to prevent automatic benefit cuts for millions of retirees.

In its agenda for the 120th Congress, TSCL called on lawmakers to:

TSCL pointed to Social Security Administration projections, which show that eliminating the taxable wage cap would add “decades” to the trust fund’s life. And the organization’s internal polling indicates broad bipartisan support among seniors for lifting the cap.

As advocacy groups push for revenue-raising reforms, a new proposal in the Senate would instead rely on federal borrowing to preserve full benefits.

Ron Johnson (R-Wis.), the chairman of the Senate Budget Committee, has introduced the Stop Scaring Seniors Act. The bill would allow the Department of the Treasury to transfer general fund dollars to Social Security’s retirement trust fund once it becomes insolvent, according to a press release published last week by the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget (CRFB).

Under current law, Social Security can only pay benefits from dedicated payroll tax income and trust fund reserves. When the retirement trust fund’s reserves are exhausted — currently projected to be in less than six years — benefits would be cut by about 22% without legislative changes.

CRFB estimated that backfilling Social Security with general revenue under Johnson’s bill would increase federal debt by $190 trillion over the next 75 years on an inflation-adjusted basis, equal to roughly 165% of gross domestic product.

“Paying for Social Security out of the general fund would absolutely explode the national debt, costing a whopping 165% of GDP over 75 years before even considering the economic implications,” CRFB President Maya MacGuineas said in the release, arguing that the policy could trigger a debt crisis or unsettle bond markets even before it is fully implemented.

CRFB characterized the bill as avoiding “the real decisions” needed to repair Social Security’s finances and urged lawmakers to pursue a mix of adjustments — potentially through a bipartisan commission — that would close the program’s funding gap without shifting the shortfall onto the federal balance sheet.

The trajectory of Social Security and Medicare benefits has direct implications for housing demand and credit risk among the senior segment.

Net benefit increases closer to 3% than 3.6% may constrain seniors’ ability to absorb higher housing costs — including the required property tax, insurance and association dues associated with reverse mortgages. The impact could be particularly acute in housing markets with rapid property tax growth.

Rising healthcare and prescription costs could drive more senior homeowners to tap their equity through home sales or reverse mortgages. Increased levels of downsizing would alter inventory and product mixes in senior-heavy markets.

A 22% across-the-board benefit cut in the next decade, if Congress fails to act, would likely raise delinquency risks among fixed-income borrowers and could affect investor views of senior-heavy mortgage-backed securities pools. Conversely, large-scale borrowing to backfill Social Security, as proposed in Johnson’s bill, could influence interest rates and broader funding conditions.

Localized affordability pressures could also emerge. Growth in senior homelessness and medical cost burdens might increase demand for affordable and supportive housing. It could also influence municipal planning, tax policy and zoning decisions that shape housing development pipelines.

by Todd Bishop on Nov 18, 2026 at 8:57 amNovember 18, 2026 at 9:01 am

Cloud-infrastructure startup Pulumi has a name for its current fiscal year, which started in July: “the year of absurd ambition.” The first results arrived Wednesday: two products the Seattle company talked about building for years but always found too big to take on.

The products, Pulumi Delivery and Pulumi Agents, let AI agents take over more of the work of getting new software up and running, and fixing it when something breaks.

“The ceiling on what we can accomplish is no longer limited by the speed at which we can build software,” said Joe Duffy, the company’s co-founder and CEO, recounting the message he delivered to the Pulumi team. “It’s limited by how ambitious we’re willing to be and how big we’re willing to dream.”

The ambition is all the more notable because Pulumi is getting smaller. The company has about 100 employees, down from about 130 last year. Duffy said there were no layoffs, and that AI has changed people’s roles and made the company more efficient.

Annual recurring revenue per employee more than doubled over the past year, he said. The company isn’t profitable yet, but it has had a few months of positive cash flow this year. Pulumi hasn’t raised money since 2023, when it landed a $41 million round led by Madrona, bringing its total to about $99 million over the company’s lifetime.

Pulumi’s co-founders include Duffy and Eric Rudder, both Microsoft veterans. They started the company in 2017 to let engineers manage cloud infrastructure such as servers, networks and permissions by writing code in everyday languages like Python and TypeScript.

The new products take that approach further:

To decide whether a change is safe to ship, Pulumi Delivery can use Jev, an AI model from TypeSafe AI that estimates the odds of specific risks the team asks about in a planned change. If a risk is higher than the threshold the team sets, the release stops.

Duffy said he first noticed TypeSafe in May when it signed up as a Pulumi customer, because he liked the name. A few months later, Jev took off and TypeSafe used Pulumi to expand worldwide.

“Now even the call on whether a change ships can be made by a model,” said Daniel Gafni, a member of the technical staff at TypeSafe AI, in the Pulumi announcement. “That’s exactly the kind of decision we built Jev to make.”

Both products are available now in public preview. Some features, including Jev decision gates and setting up agents, require Pulumi’s paid Pro or Enterprise plans.

Lucky timing: Pulumi’s founding bet on everyday programming languages turned out to suit AI agents, which are trained to be very good at writing exactly that kind of code.

“I wish I could say I predicted that 10 years ago, but it turns out in this case, what’s good for humans is also good for agents,” Duffy said.

AI agents now handle 40% of the operations on the Pulumi platform that people used to do, up from 15% in April and none in January, Duffy said. Agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Pulumi’s own Neo are making infrastructure changes on their own.

Duffy said many companies building AI coding tools stop once the code is written and reviewed. “For them, life stops at the merge,” he said. The new products cover the steps after that, from testing through release.

Plenty of company: Pulumi won’t have this market to itself. Duffy pointed to Harness, which calls it the “agentic SDLC” (short for software development lifecycle), and GitHub, which pitched “agentic software delivery” at its Universe conference last month. He said Cursor aspires to solve the problem and Anthropic built its own internal system.

The new products could replace some of the work now done by tools such as Argo CD and GitHub Actions, along with lots of homegrown scripts, he said.

“This is an industry-changing moment, and somebody has to solve this problem,” Duffy said. “And I think we are exceptionally well poised to do so.”

Bring your own bot: Neo, the infrastructure agent Pulumi introduced last year, is now just one example of a Pulumi agent. Customers can set up as many as they want, each with its own job, instructions and tools. They can also bring their own agent, such as Claude Code or Codex, and run it in Pulumi’s cloud.

Neo itself, which ran mainly on Anthropic’s Claude, can now use models from OpenAI or Google, too. “It’s not just Anthropic anymore,” Duffy said.

Agents can start work from an alert in PagerDuty, Datadog or Honeycomb, on a schedule or on request, and they report back to teams in Slack.

Pulumi has briefed about 50 customers, and about a dozen are in a private beta. Duffy said no launch in the company’s history has gotten a warmer reception, and he named Moderna among the customers eager to get it.

Pulumi has thousands of customers overall, including major companies such as BMW, Snowflake and Wiz.

The business: Pulumi’s gross margins have stayed in the high 80s to low 90s even as agents drive up usage, Duffy said. Many customers run Pulumi from inside their own Claude Code sessions, which means they’re paying both Anthropic and Pulumi.

Duffy said Pulumi wasn’t out looking for money when it raised its last two rounds. Investors came to the company, and each deal came together in about 48 hours.

Madrona’s Tim Porter has joined the board, Duffy said, taking the seat previously held by the late Soma Somasegar, who led Pulumi’s first investment.

About 40 of the company’s 100 employees are in the Seattle area, working out of an office at Two Union Square. Duffy said Pulumi is hiring more people locally because in-person work still matters when building new products.

Despite the smaller headcount, Pulumi is still hiring, including sales reps in nearly every region of the world. Inside the company, Duffy said Pulumi is having a lot of success with “product-minded engineers who can think from our customers’ point of view, who can think like engineering managers, commanding a team of agents.”

Asked whether a sale or more funding was in the cards, Duffy said Pulumi aspires to be a long-term successful business. “There are a variety of ways to get there,” he said. “But we want to get there on our own terms.”

#5376. NOAH HOLDINGS LIMITED ANNOUNCES UNAUDITED FINANCIAL RESULTS FOR THE THIRD QUARTER OF 2026

SINGAPORE, Nov. 24, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Noah Holdings Limited ("Noah" or the "Company") (NYSE: NOAH and HKEX: 6686), a leading and pioneer wealth management service provider offering comprehensive one-stop advisory services on global investment and asset allocation primarily for global Chinese high-net-worth investors, today announced its unaudited financial results for the third quarter of 2026.

The Company reports its operational performance across six business segments â three mainland China and three international[2] â plus headquarters. The following updates provide segment-specific operating metrics and developments during the third quarter of 2026.

[1] Noah's Non-GAAP financial measures are its corresponding GAAP financial measures excluding the effects of all forms of share-based compensation, impact related to settlements and net of relevant tax impact, if any. See "Reconciliation of GAAP to Non-GAAP Results" at the end of this press release.[2] For classification of the Group's business segments for the purposes of this announcement, "international" refers to business activities conducted in, or relating to, countries and regions outside Mainland China.[3] "Active clients" for a given period refers to registered investors who purchase investment products distributed or receive services provided by us during that given period.

[4] "Other products" refers to other investment products, which includes insurance products, multi-strategies products and others.[5] The asset allocation/redemption of international investment products includes the fluctuation result of foreign currencies exchange rate.[6] The asset allocation/redemption of public securities also includes market appreciation or depreciation.

Our Mainland China operations are organized into three reportable segments: mainland China public securities, mainland China asset management, and mainland China insurance. Each segment operates under a dedicated brand and serves a distinct client need in the mainland China market.

Mainland China public securities, operating under the Noah Upright brand, is the business that distributes mutual funds and private secondary products in mainland China. This segment operates under an "online-first, offline-supported" business model, with the goal of facilitating global asset allocation through RMB-denominated products.

Mainland China asset management, operating under the Gopher Asset Management brand, is the business that manages RMB-denominated private equity funds and private secondary products. Current focus areas include managing primary market exits on existing vintages and growing cross-border ETF products in the secondary market.

Mainland China insurance, operating under the Glory brand, is the business that distributes insurance products in mainland China, consisting mainly of life and health insurance products. The business has been undergoing a strategic shift toward a commission-only broker model and comprehensive family succession planning services. The net revenues for the third quarter of 2026 were RMB1.3 million (US$0.2 million).

Our international operations are organized into three reportable segments: international wealth management, international asset management, and international insurance and comprehensive services. The Company operates booking centers in Hong Kong, Singapore and key U.S. markets including New York, Los Angeles and Silicon Valley.

International wealth management, operating under the ARK Wealth Management brand, is the business that provides offline and online wealth management services to global Chinese high-net-worth investors outside mainland China. Currently we are dedicated to providing comprehensive services using our booking centers in Hong Kong and Singapore.

International asset management, operating under the Olive Asset Management brand, is the business that manages USD-denominated private equity funds and private secondary products, with a dedicated U.S. product center and partnerships with top-tier global managers across structured products and hedge funds. We are building our offices in Hong Kong, Singapore, Japan and key U.S. markets, including New York and Silicon Valley.

International insurance and comprehensive services

International insurance and comprehensive services, operating under the Glory Family Heritage brand, is the business that provides comprehensive international services such as insurance distribution, trust services and other family office-style services. With offices in Hong Kong, Singapore and Los Angeles, we provide global coverage to clients.

Headquarters reflects revenue generated from corporate operations at the Company's headquarters in Singapore and office in Shanghai, as well as administrative costs and expenses that are not directly allocated to the aforementioned six business segments, including investments in platform-wide technology, AI infrastructure and corporate functions.

"In the third quarter of 2026, global markets became more volatile, and many high-net-worth clients shifted toward caution, liquidity and diversification," commented Ms. Jingbo Wang, Co-founder and Chairwoman of Noah. "We used this period to reposition the business. We stayed with our decision to step back from insurance distribution and put our resources into investment products and global asset allocation, where our long-term strengths lie. Even as markets pulled back, demand for our investment products held up, and our overseas business continued to deliver steady contributions."

"This quarter's results also include several one-off costs from streamlining our organization. We see these as investments in a leaner, more focused Noah."

"Building on the foundation we set out in the first half of the year, our use of AI is enhancing both the quality of our client service and the efficiency of our organization. It allows our relationship managers to serve more clients with greater consistency and helps our four global booking centers work together more seamlessly. Looking ahead, we will keep strengthening our global platform, risk management and technology capabilities to create long-term value for our clients and shareholders."

Net revenues for the third quarter of 2026 were RMB509.0 million (US$75.9 million), a 19.6% decrease from the corresponding period in 2025, primarily due to lower one-time commissions from international insurance distribution and lower recurring service fees from mainland China private equity products, partially offset by higher performance-based income from mainland China private secondary products.

Net revenues under the segmentation[7] are as follows:

International insurance and comprehensive services

These are changes in segment names only and do not involve any material change in the nature or scope of the underlying business activities included in the respective segments. Accordingly, the financial and operating information presented under the renamed segments remains comparable to the corresponding information previously presented under the former segment names.

Operating costs and expenses for the third quarter of 2026 were RMB445.1 million (US$66.4 million), a 3.5% decrease from the corresponding period in 2025. Operating costs and expenses for the third quarter of 2026 primarily consisted of (i) compensation and benefits of RMB270.0 million (US$40.3 million); (ii) selling expenses of RMB54.1 million (US$8.1 million); (iii) general and administrative expenses of RMB87.4 million (US$13.0 million); (iv) provision for credit losses of RMB2.9 million (US$0.4 million); (v) other operating expenses of RMB31.0 million (US$4.6 million); less (vi) income from government subsidies of RMB0.3 million (US$0.05 million).

Operating margin for the third quarter of 2026 was 12.6%, compared with 27.2% for the corresponding period in 2025.

Interest income for the third quarter of 2026 was RMB29.5 million (US$4.4 million), a 2.8% increase from the corresponding period in 2025.

Investment income for the third quarter of 2026 was RMB85.5 million (US$12.7 million), compared with RMB20.6 million in the corresponding period in 2025, primarily due to higher fair value gains on investments held by consolidated funds.

Income tax expense for the third quarter of 2026 was RMB62.1 million (US$9.3 million), an 8.0% decrease from the corresponding period in 2025.

Non-GAAP Net Income Attributable to Noah Shareholders

As of September 30, 2026, the Company had RMB3,891.7 million (US$580.5 million) in cash and cash equivalents, compared with RMB4,322.7 million as of June 30, 2026 and RMB3,837.4 million as of September 30, 2025.

Net cash inflow from the Company's operating activities during the third quarter of 2026 was RMB175.0 million (US$26.1 million), compared with a net cash inflow of RMB316.9 million in the corresponding period in 2025. The decrease was primarily due to lower income from operations and decreases in contingent liabilities.

Net cash inflow from the Company's investing activities during the third quarter of 2026 was RMB32.3 million (US$4.8 million), compared with a net cash inflow of RMB253.7 million in the corresponding period in 2025. The decrease was primarily due to lower net proceeds from redemptions of held-to-maturity investments.

Net cash outflow from the Company's financing activities during the third quarter of 2026 was RMB612.0 million (US$91.3 million), compared with a net cash outflow of RMB549.9 million in the corresponding period in 2025, primarily due to higher dividend payments.

#5375. Key insights from HPE’s Q4 earnings report

ANALYSIS by Zeus Kerravala

Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co.delivered a record fiscal fourth quarter this week, roughly doubling its fiscal 2027 growth outlook, but its stock gave back nearly all of the prior day’s rally. The selloff suggests Wall Street still prices HPE as a low-margin server vendor, even though the results describe a networking and artificial intelligence infrastructure company with demand exceeding its ability to ship.

Fourth-quarter revenue rose 50%, to $14.5 billion, orders grew 88%, and adjusted earnings of $1.43 per share topped the high end of guidance. HPE now expects fiscal 2027 revenue to grow 27% to 35%, with adjusted earnings of $5.05 to $5.35 per share, according to its earnings release.

I joined a briefing with Chief Executive Antonio Neri and a small group of independent analysts shortly before the results came out. Here are my four takeaways for investors and information technology leaders:

Neri explained that networking orders grew more than 4.5 times faster than networking revenue in the quarter, up from 3.5 times the quarter before, and HPE exited the year with $10.5 billion in AI backlog.

HPE doubled its networking purchase commitments over the summer and raised them again in the fourth quarter, but those components carry lead times of 28 to 40-plus weeks, so Neri expects networking conversion to pick up starting in the second quarter. Supply constraints are a better problem to have than weak demand, but they mean fiscal 2027 hinges on converting orders rather than winning them.

The Juniper Networks integration is complete, and the annual cost-synergy target has risen to $800 million, but the bigger story remains the profit mix. Chief Financial Officer Marie Myers said networking will account for more than 40% of HPE’s operating profit by the fourth quarter of fiscal 2027, up from less than a quarter of revenue. AI is a major driver, with routing orders growing by triple digits as customers connect AI data centers to one another.

Security was the soft spot, which Neri called “just timing.” When I asked whether the security portfolio is where he wants it as the industry consolidates around big platforms, he argued for a different path.

“Fortinet and we have a different strategy — the convergence of security and networking — and we are taking it all the way down to the silicon level,” he said. The convergence of networking and security is underway but will take time to execute, as a considerable amount of technical debt must go through its depreciation cycle. In a greenfield situation, organizations can easily deploy a converged solution, but in a brownfield environment, it requires much more work. This is the right strategy, but it remains a “prove-it” business for HPE.

Many neoclouds rely on vendor financing and chip-backed debt, raising real concerns about who is left exposed if the buildout slows. HPE says it has stayed out, and Neri was quite emphatic about it on the briefing.

“I want to be clear: We have not financed any neocloud through HPFS, our financing arm,” he said. “We have zero exposure to any AI financing for neocloud.” HPE has likely left some revenue on the table, but it drew the line in the right place. It will sell to neoclouds, as its $1.2 billion Vultr order shows, without acting as their bank. Enterprise and sovereign customers account for the majority of its cumulative AI orders, and if the neocloud financing chain breaks, HPE’s financing arm won’t be the one holding the paper.

Training built the first phase of AI infrastructure, and Neri believes inference will build the next and will dominate demand for AI infrastructure. “I believe by the end of the decade, 80% will be in AI inferencing,” he said. “Much of that will land on-prem. Much of that will be distributed, for sure. That’s why the server business is structurally well-positioned.”

Once agents are in production, token costs become a recurring bill, and companies will want inference running alongside their own data. Those servers require far more memory and pull in storage and services, which is better business than racking graphics processing units for a hyperscaler.

Evidence of this is the interest in Helios, the Advanced Microdevices Inc. rack that uses HPE’s Ethernet switching rather than Nvidia’s proprietary interconnect. I asked Neri whether Jensen Huang’s brief departure from Nvidia Corp. had opened that door. He said interest was building before then, as customers look to diversify.

HPE shares jumped 17% on Monday ahead of the report as part of a broader AI rally, then fell about 13% in early trading on Tuesday, ending near where they started the week. I see three reasons for this.

The first is margins. Cloud & AI operating margin was 18.4% in the quarter, and HPE guided to about 14% for fiscal 2027. Reuters reported that JPMorgan analysts called margin mix the key debate for investors.

The second is pricing. Myers said higher selling prices have been the biggest driver of server growth, and she expects gross margin to moderate in the second half as AI server volumes ramp and costs rise faster than pricing.

The third is timing. HPE expects about 54% of revenue in the second half, with the ramp tied to Helios shipments, the Oracle Corp. deal, customer data center readiness and component supply. Those are fair execution questions, but they miss the shift in where HPE’s profit comes from.

On the topic of margins, the 18.4% came off an unusual stretch of favorable pricing that should not have been modeled as permanent. Neri argued the guide is still “significantly higher than any historical margin we have had in this business,” and he’s right outside the past year. A year ago, the segment’s margin was 9.3%. Margin rate also isn’t margin dollars. At 30% to 40% revenue growth, my math shows Cloud & AI adding well over $1 billion in operating profit at the midpoint.

The bears are right that price-driven server growth doesn’t warrant a premium multiple, which is why the mix matters more. The market is fixated on the segment whose margins are normalizing and ignoring the one whose margins are expanding. Adjusted earnings per share are still guided to grow by 27% to 35%, in line with revenue growth. That’s far from the margin doom-and-gloom narrative on the stock.

The back-half concern is real but manageable. Myers described the pipeline as multiples of the backlog, and Neri said the guide assumes only historical win rates against it.

Then there’s quality. HPE is guiding to about 30% growth and at least $5.5 billion in free cash flow, has no neocloud financing exposure and has already brought leverage below its target. It trades at about eight times the midpoint of its adjusted earnings guidance. “I don’t see us at a multiple that is 8 to 9x; it makes no sense whatsoever,” Neri said on the earnings call.

For old HPE, that’s true, as it’s a server vendor, but HPE is increasingly a network vendor each quarter. In fact, during our pre-call with Neri, he led with networking and spoke at length about the business before pivoting to the server business. Expect networking to continue to drive a larger share of profits.

Fiscal 2027 is an execution year. HPE must convert purchase commitments into shipments, ramp Helios and prove that networking margins can climb even as cloud and AI margins settle. I’ll be watching networking order conversion more closely than server margins. If HPE executes, today’s multiple will prove to be too low.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#5374. BTR sector fears Treasury rules move the goal line on investor ban

Treasury closed public comments on proposed ROAD act rules for build-to-rent exemptions to the institutional investor ban. Industry groups opposed the 18-month certificate-of-occupancy purchase window and sought clearer definitions for single-plat communities and rehab exceptions.  AI Summary

Earlier this year, build-to-rent projects secured some notable exemptions from the institutional investor ban included in the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act. However, while the industry still doesn’t know exactly what the final rules will look like, it just moved a step closer to finding out.

Monday marked the end of the U.S. Department of the Treasury‘s public comment period on its proposed rules for BTR exemptions from the institutional investor ban. Although ROAD explicitly exempted BTR from the ban, some of the proposed rules and language Treasury released in October have left the industry uneasy and unsure of where it stands.

BTR developers and operators say this uncertainty continues to suppress capital flowing into new projects, a trend they expect to continue until the federal government clarifies the rules.

Last month, Treasury released a notice of proposed rulemaking detailing how it would implement the institutional investor ban while protecting BTR communities. The proposed rules would exempt newly built, never-owner-occupied BTR communities if an investor buys them within 18 months of receiving a certificate of occupancy and uses them only as rentals.

Treasury would also exempt communities that include both rental and for-sale homes, allowing builders to sell the rental portion to large institutional investors while marketing the remaining homes to individual buyers. The proposals additionally call for allowing transfers of existing BTR communities between large institutional investors and keeping the renovate-to-rent exemption.

Although the rules appear to protect BTR, industry leaders say the finer details leave several concerns unresolved.

“If you read the law as a layman, you’d say, ‘all right, built-to-rent is carved out.’ But then you get this rulemaking, and it’s like you have to pat your belly and tap your head and hop on one foot for the built-to-rent to not be banned,” Sean Dobson, chairman, CEO and CIO at The Amherst Group, said in an interview with HousingWire TBD.

Over the last month, Treasury received more than 450 letters with questions and concerns concerning its proposed rulemakings. HousingWire TBD reviewed 10 of those letters, from high-profile BTR developers and operators and leading organizations that advocate on behalf of the rental housing industry, including:

These letters detailed the outstanding concerns that the industry still has concerning how Treasury will enforce ROAD. With the institutional investor ban set to take effect on January 7, Treasury has several weeks to finalize and release the rules that BTR operators will have to follow.

Until then, the industry has to wait and see whether, and how, those concerns are addressed.

The chief concern among BTR developers, operators and advocates is the proposed requirement that institutional investors purchase BTR communities within 18 months of receiving a certificate of occupancy (CO). Under the proposed framework, if a developer fails to sell a community by that deadline, they may lose the ability to do so altogether.

That proposal matters because many BTR developers, much like multifamily developers, rely on selling their communities after completion and stabilization to make a profit and move on to their next project.

Richard Ross, CEO at Quinn Residences, argued that the 18-month window is far too limiting. A community may still be under development and lease-up after the first homes receive a CO, so 18 months will almost certainly run out before the full community is ready to sell.

“To build and stabilize a new community takes about 30 months. If I start receiving certificates of occupancy at month 15, I may not receive the final CO for the last home until month 28 or 29. I need enough time to complete and stabilize the entire community before selling it,” Ross said in an interview.

The letters that HousingWire TBD reviewed unanimously opposed the proposed 18-month window. Just like Ross, industry groups argued that the deadline does not align with how rental communities are developed, leased up, financed and sold.

The letter signed by a coalition of 12 BTR developers led by Greystar and Brookfield Residential argued that the deadline would create uncertainty for projects that may not be sold until years after construction. The letter further argued the restrictions would continue to affect financing decisions for future projects.

“A smaller potential buyer pool reduces liquidity and creates greater uncertainty regarding terminal value,” the letter read.

Additionally, the groups argued that Treasury must protect long-term institutional owners’ ability to purchase BTR communities. Otherwise, the federal government would undermine the industry.

“If large institutional investors cannot purchase horizontal multifamily communities (which individual families cannot), the values of those properties will fall and new construction and necessary maintenance and reinvestment will slow,” MBA’s letter read.

To address this, NAA and NMHC, two of the largest rental housing advocacy organizations, requested that Treasury eliminate the deadline or replace it with a provision that institutional investors can purchase BTR communities directly from the builder or developer responsible for construction.

Quinn Residences, AHV Communities and LGI Homes also requested that Treasury remove or substantially extend the deadline. LGI Homes also emphasized the need for production homebuilders to retain the option of renting homes that have not sold.

Treasury’s proposed rulemaking describes the three activities that could qualify an institutional investor as a covered entity as “purchases, constructs, or constructs and retains”. This matters because BTR developers often build and retain homes as rental properties before selling stabilized communities to finance future developments.

Treasury’s language is ambiguous, leaving open the possibility that BTR developers could be treated like institutional investors.

The National Rental Home Council made this a central argument in its letter, distinguishing between an investor buying a home from someone else and one acting as the builder. The organization urged Treasury to recognize that developers who build and retain homes as rentals operate differently from investors who purchase newly built homes from third parties.

Up for Growth Action made a similar argument, urging Treasury to differentiate between creating new rental housing and acquiring existing housing.

Several letters argued that Treasury’s proposed rule does not clearly distinguish single-plat rental communities, where multiple homes share one parcel and common ownership, from individual single-family homes. They worry the rule could inadvertently restrict the development, ownership or sale of these communities by treating them as collections of individual homes subject to the institutional investor ban.

In response, BTR advocates argued for clearer rules for single-plat communities and those mixing renters and owners, while NRHC asked whether buildings with three or more attached units could count as single-family homes.

The letters also raise concerns about the proposed exception for investors that purchase distressed homes, substantially rehabilitate them and rent them out. Treasury’s proposed rules would allow institutional investors to purchase existing homes in need of extensive repairs, as long as they spend 15% of the purchase price on improvements.

However, several of the letters argued that the 15% threshold is too high. They further argued that the rule could be hard to enforce for homes that are difficult to inspect before purchase, homes in jurisdictions without applicable local codes, and homes with problems that aren’t obvious upfront.

Rental housing advocates disagreed on how flexible the rehabilitation threshold should be. While some groups advocated for increasing the threshold, NMHC, NAA and RETTC support the 15% benchmark while advocating for more flexibility in identifying problems and applying older building standards.

The common theme is that industry leaders want the exception to work for genuinely distressed properties without requiring investors to predict every hidden problem before purchasing a home.

Several letters raise implementation issues beyond those five main concerns, including:

#5372. IntraFi Cofounder and CEO Mark Jacobsen Named EY Entrepreneur Of The Year in Financial Services

Recognition honors Jacobsen's invention of reciprocal deposits and nearly 25 years of innovation, helping banks compete and serve their communities

ARLINGTON, Va., Nov. 24, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Mark P. Jacobsen, Cofounder and CEO of IntraFi, was named an EY Entrepreneur Of The YearÂ® 2026 National Award winner in the Financial Services category, recognizing his pioneering contributions to the banking industry and his leadership in building the nation's largest reciprocal deposit network.

The recognition celebrates Jacobsen's contributions to helping community and regional banks attract and retain deposits, allowing them to grant access for their customers to aggregate higher levels of FDIC insurance coverage and enabling them to better serve their communities.

Nearly 25 years ago, Jacobsen recognized a challenge facing community banks and their customers. Businesses and municipalities often needed to maintain deposits exceeding traditional FDIC insurance limits, while smaller banks struggled to compete with larger institutions for those relationships.

Jacobsen "conceived the idea of reciprocal deposits," wrote EY in its recognition. "IntraFi created an entirely new banking product."

Reciprocal deposit services allow community banks to place uninsured deposits through a deposit placement network in increments below FDIC insurance limits and receive a matching amount of insured deposits in return. This allows small businesses, public funds and nonprofits to obtain higher levels of aggregate FDIC insurance. This benefits both the bank and its customers, allowing depositors to have a single relationship with their preferred institution while the bank can use the full amount of the deposit to fuel economic growth.

"Jacobsen brought the idea to life by combining a regulator's understanding of the financial system and an entrepreneur's instinct to challenge conventional thinking, plus the resolve to see the challenge through," said EY, noting Jacobsen's former role as the chief of staff of two federal banking regulators. "He earned a dozen patents and worked with all the federal banking agencies as well as state and local governments, prompting more than 40 state laws to enable the use of reciprocal deposits."

Today, IntraFi operates the nation's largest reciprocal deposit network, connecting more than 3,000 financial institutions, the vast majority of which are community banks. IntraFi's scale, sophisticated infrastructure, and proven reliability distinguish it from other providers, with established systems that have supported banks through multiple financial crises and periods of market stress.

"Any recognition belongs solely to the employees of IntraFi and the thousands of banks that have put their faith in us," said Jacobsen. "We built this network bank by bank with a commitment to do things the right way, not relying on marketing puffery or short-lived promises. And we remain committed to constant innovation. Whether it's helping community banks compete for deposits or exploring how our network could support the next generation of payments, our goal remains the same: giving banks the tools they need to better serve their customers."

IntraFi's unmatched network scale and proven operational reliability reinforces its position as a trusted partner to banks of all sizes.

The EY Entrepreneur Of The Year program recognizes entrepreneurs whose innovation, leadership, and vision have transformed industries and created lasting economic and community impact.

IntraFi has built the largest financial network of its kind, connecting thousands of financial institutions nationwide. The company is the nation's leading provider of reciprocal deposit services and a leading provider of overnight and term funding options. IntraFi helps financial institutions manage liquidity, access funding, and provide customers with solutions for keeping large deposits safe.

IntraFi is not an FDIC-insured bank, and deposit insurance covers the failure of an insured bank. A list identifying IntraFi network banks appears at https://www.intrafi.com/network-banks. Certain conditions must be satisfied for "pass-through" FDIC deposit insurance coverage to apply. Use of an IntraFi service is subject to the terms, conditions, and disclosures in the applicable program agreements.

#5371. Latest findings point to fuel supply, not Blue Origin’s engines, in loss of Amazon Leo satellites

by Todd Bishop on Nov 18, 2026 at 10:01 amNovember 18, 2026 at 10:08 am

Blue Origin’s engines look like they’re off the hook, at least for now.

The two BE-4 engines Blue Origin makes for United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket weren’t to blame for the low thrust in Sunday’s failed launch, according to preliminary findings released Wednesday. Instead, it appears the engines didn’t get enough fuel from the rocket, ULA said.

In its latest update on the investigation, ULA said it had completed an initial integrated review of flight data. Preliminary data indicate the first stage’s low thrust came from “inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines,” ULA said, adding that work remains to determine the cause.

On Tuesday, ULA said early data suggested the first stage underperformed just after liftoff, leaving the rocket too low and too slow to put 40 of Amazon’s Leo internet satellites into orbit. It didn’t say then whether the engines played a role.

The BE-4s are made by Jeff Bezos’ Kent, Wash.-based Blue Origin. Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp said Wednesday on X that he was proud of the BE-4 team for its “rapid response and support of ULA’s investigation” and that the company looks forward to Vulcan’s return to flight.

The finding matters for Blue Origin beyond Vulcan. Its own New Glenn rocket uses seven BE-4s on its first stage, and Amazon has 24 New Glenn launches reserved for Leo.

ULA repeated that Vulcan’s second stage appears to have started normally and that its RL10 engines operated as planned but couldn’t make up for the earlier loss of performance. The six Northrop Grumman solid rocket boosters, the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appear to have performed normally, ULA said.

The Federal Aviation Administration is overseeing the ULA-led investigation. Amazon’s next Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission carrying 36 satellites, targeted for no earlier than Nov. 23 from French Guiana.

ULA said it will share more as the investigation continues.

"It's exciting to be part of something that's growing while making a difference in the lives of children."

DiGilio taught second grade for 23 years before founding Laprea. The company now serves more than 800 school districts in all 50 states, employs about 50 people, and was named to the Inc. 5000 list of America's fastest-growing private companies in 2025 and 2026. DiGilio was also named to the 2026 Inc. Female Founders 500.

Earlier in his career, he spent more than a decade at Microsoft over two stints, most recently leading teams that served the Azure Partner Experience group.

Ethereum vs. Solana in 2027: Elon Musk’s Grok AI predicts which is positioned for bigger gains at the end of this article. As of mid-November 2026, Ethereum (ETH) trades near $1,780–$1,880 with a market cap of about $210–$230Bn, while Solana (SOL) trades near $65–$80 with a market cap of roughly $35-45Bn.

Both have endured sharp drawdowns from prior peaks: ETH is roughly 63% below its August 2025 high near $4,946, and SOL is about 75% below its January 2025 peak near $293.

In a potential 2027 recovery, percentage gains favor the higher-beta asset with clearer near-term execution catalysts. Solana appears better positioned for larger relative upside, though Ethereum retains advantages in institutional depth and lower relative risk.

ETH remains in a broader downtrend, trading below key moving averages. Recent data place it below its 20-day, 50-day, and often the 200-day averages (near $2,100–$2,150 in recent readings). Support has been tested around $1,750–$2,000, with deeper levels near the August 2026 lows or the one-year trough.

Resistance clusters near the 200-day MA and prior recovery highs in the mid-$2,000s. Volume and momentum indicators reflect caution: ETH has shown more muted rebounds than SOL in several 2026 bottoms, consistent with its larger market cap and institutional ownership base.

Spot ETF flows provide a structural bid, but on-chain activity and Layer-2 fee dynamics need to reaccelerate for sustained upside. A decisive close above the 200-day MA would signal trend improvement, opening paths toward $3,000–$4,000+ in a constructive environment, though percentage gains from current levels would likely trail more volatile peers.

SOL exhibits higher volatility and stronger historical rebound characteristics in the current cycle. It has delivered larger percentage recoveries from multiple 2026 lows (including a notable ~64% bounce from an August trough in one instance) compared with ETH.

Price currently sits below its 200-day moving average (recently cited near $89), with near-term support around $60–$70 and resistance at that MA and higher levels toward $100–$140. The chart structure shows sharper declines but also sharper recoveries, typical of a smaller-cap asset with intense retail and DeFi participation.

Momentum can shift quickly on positive network news. A sustained close above the 200-day MA would mark a meaningful technical improvement and support double-digit percentage gains from current prices in a broad risk-on environment. Downside risks remain elevated if support near prior cycle lows fails.

Explore: The Best Token Presales Right Now

Ethereum’s roadmap centers on continued scaling and resilience. The Glamsterdam upgrade (featuring enshrined proposer-builder separation/ePBS and block-level access lists) has faced testnet delays and may slip into early 2027.

It aims to support higher gas limits (potentially toward 200 million) and better parallelization. Hegotá, targeted for 2027, includes FOCIL for stronger censorship resistance. Broader themes include Layer-2 maturation, real-world asset (RWA) and tokenization growth, account abstraction progress, and early post-quantum research discussions (with some proposals accelerating timelines).

Institutional catalysts remain strong: established spot ETFs, deep stablecoin and DeFi liquidity, and Ethereum’s role as settlement infrastructure. Successful delivery of capacity upgrades and sustained ETF inflows could drive meaningful appreciation, though the network’s maturity means percentage gains may be more measured than those of faster-growing competitors.

Solana’s 2026–2027 catalysts emphasize performance and reliability. Firedancer (Jump Crypto’s independent validator client) continues mainnet rollout, improving client diversity, efficiency, and throughput headroom.

Alpenglow, the consensus overhaul targeting finality near 150 milliseconds (from ~12.8 seconds), has advanced through governance and testing, with mainnet activation expected in the near term.

Additional work includes compute limit adjustments and post-quantum signature research. Real-world adoption catalysts stand out: DTCC plans to connect its tokenization service to Solana in the second half of 2027.

Other drivers include tokenized equities and assets, payments activity, DeFi volume leadership in certain categories, declining inflation schedule, and existing spot ETFs.

These factors, combined with Solana’s low fees and high throughput, position it well for consumer and high-frequency use cases that could accelerate demand in a recovery.

Solana is more likely to deliver the larger percentage gains in 2027. Its smaller market capitalization, higher historical beta, and concrete performance upgrades (Firedancer + Alpenglow) create greater asymmetry if risk appetite returns and network activity expands.

Analyst scenarios often show wider upside ranges for SOL relative to current levels compared with ETH. Ethereum offers a more stable institutional foundation and could post solid absolute returns on successful upgrades and RWA growth, but its larger size typically compresses percentage upside.

Both face risks: macro headwinds, execution delays, competition, and residual network reliability questions for Solana. Crypto markets remain highly uncertain; past performance and roadmaps are not guarantees.

Investors should weigh risk tolerance carefully. In a constructive 2027 backdrop, Solana’s combination of technical momentum potential and upcoming catalysts gives it the edge for the strongest relative gains.

#5366. ‘Sister isn’t free’: Melinda French Gates fact-checks viral ‘SNL’ sketch on eldercare

Geek Life: Fun stories, memes, humor and other random items at the intersection of tech, science, business and culture.  SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 18, 2026 at 1:23 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 1:23 pm

A “Saturday Night Live” skit about caring for aging relatives touched a viral nerve after it aired over the weekend, including with Melinda French Gates, who offered her own “fact check” on the too-close-to-home comedy.

The sketch, a fake commercial, stars host John Mulaney as a man who has found an easy way to care for his aging father without upending his own life: “Sister,” an “elder care system” that is free and is, in fact, his sister.

French Gates wrote on Instagram this week that the sketch “is funny because it’s a little too true.” Using research from Pivotal, her investment and philanthropic organization, she went through the ad’s claims one by one and found that most held up:

Sister will provide. True, French Gates said, citing AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving. Among adults ages 55 to 64, women are nearly 40% more likely than men to care for an older relative, and nearly 40% more likely to provide constant care.

She’ll quit her job. “Mostly true,” at least the job part. Catalyst found that 42% of women who voluntarily left jobs in 2025 cited caregiving as the main reason.

Paid help is pricey. “True, unfortunately.” New America puts the average home health aide at more than $6,600 a month, and 24-hour care can top $25,000.

Sister may break down. Also true. In the Caregiving in the U.S. 2025 report, nearly two-thirds of caregivers said they were under moderate or high emotional stress, and women felt the strain more than men did.

“Free” is misleading. French Gates said Sister isn’t free; she’s the one paying for the care, in lost wages, stalled careers, thinner retirement savings and less time for her own life.

French Gates has made women’s health and caregiving central to her work since she stepped down as co-chair of the Gates Foundation in 2024.

She left with $12.5 billion to put toward her work on behalf of women and families. Much of that work runs through Pivotal, the Seattle-area organization she founded to handle her philanthropy and investments. In June she pledged another $215 million for women’s health, which brought her giving in that area to more than $600 million over two years. The pledge included $10 million to the Menopause Society for better menopause care in the U.S.

The sketch has been shared widely across the country this week, in part because it lines up so closely with the research.

In its own analysis, The New York Times cited studies showing that daughters generally provide at least twice as much care to aging parents as sons do. The U.S., unlike many wealthy countries, offers no federal paid leave or long-term care insurance for family caregivers.

French Gates said she welcomed the conversation.

“I’m so glad we’re talking about this, and laughing about it,” she wrote on Instagram. “We need more honesty about what caring for loved ones really takes and why so much of that work falls to women. But I’d love for the day to come when these jokes don’t pack quite the same punch — because we’ve made it so much easier to care for the people we love.”

#5365. Congress scrutinizes Jensen Huang’s return as Megaspeed restrictions raise questions

Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have criticized Nvidia Corp.’s decision to rehire Jensen Huang as its chief executive.

The criticism came against the backdrop of a controversial move by the U.S. Commerce Department. The agency applied new export restrictions to Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud operator. The company played a prominent role in the spy controversy that led to Huang’s resignation. According to trade experts, the Commerce Department left out a key clause that is usually included in such restrictions.

Huang resigned on Nov. 12 following revelations that he had an affair with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive. Early reporting about the relationship indicated that she was found to have passed intelligence to China. The U.S. Justice Department later stated that it has not yet reached a conclusion on whether Alice Huang is a spy. Earlier this week, the New York Times reported that she maintained contact with a Chinese intelligence official.

Nvidia’s board reinstated Jensen Huang on Monday after U.S. President Donald Trump and tech industry figures urged directors to bring him back. The move drew widespread criticism from members of Congress.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-New York), who is set to become House Speaker, called the reinstatement “indefensible, irresponsible and incomprehensible.” Rep. Don Bacon (R-Nebraska), the chair of House Subcommittee on Cyber, Information Technologies and Innovation, said that “it’s inexplicable to me why they want this guy back as CEO.”

Multiple lawmakers told CNBC that they plan to closely scrutinize Huang’s conduct. The executive is scheduled to testify before multiple Congressional committees next Tuesday. Furthermore, Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore) told the outlet that Democrats plan to scrutinize the Trump administration’s role in the matter.

The Commerce Department today added Megaspeed and several of its regional affiliates to its Entity List. Companies on the list can only purchase sensitive products such as graphics cards if they obtain a license from the U.S. government. According to Gizmodo, the move has drawn scrutiny because the restrictions applied to Megaspeed include a loophole.

All the companies on the Entity List are prohibited from buying Nvidia’s latest chips unless they secure a license. Most of them are also unable to buy lower-end graphics cards, high-bandwidth memory and related hardware. The latter restrictions are specified in a clause called the FDPR provision. The Commerce Department has reportedly not applied the FDPR provision to Megaspeed when it added the company to the Entity List.

Huang returned to Nvidia’s Santa Clara, Calif. headquarters on Monday. The news sent the chipmaker’s stock soaring more than 30%, although it parred some of the gains today. Nvidia shares are down 5.8% from Monday.

Wired today published excerpts from Huang’s all-hands meeting with employees. The executive apologized for his affairs and for his management style, which has also come under scrutiny in recent days. He added that he will undergo a “360-degree review” and that Nvidia’s code of conduct is still in effect.

#5364. Preserve the Pensions Project to Digitize War of 1812 Pension Files is Now Complete

Valuable Records are Available for Free Online

SILVER SPRING, Md. , Nov. 24, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The National Genealogical Society (NGS) is excited to share that the Preserve the Pensions project to digitize War of 1812 pension files is finished, and the files are now available to the public for free permanently with full-text search via Fold3.

The culmination of sixteen years of fundraising and careful work to save deteriorating files and make them accessible online, this project provides genealogists and family historians with nearly three million pages of records from approximately 90,000 individual files. A partnership between NGS, Fold3, Ancestry, FamilySearch, and the National Archives and Records Administration (NARA), and contributions from people and organizations across the genealogy community, made this incredible endeavor possible and illustrate the power of collaboration.

"After successfully raising the $2.7 million needed to conserve and digitize the War of 1812 pensions deposited with NARA in Washington, DC, we are thrilled that our digitization partner, Fold3, has completed digitizing the last box of pensions. This effort, originally initiated as a request from the National Archives, concludes the largest private/public partnership the genealogical community has had where donations led directly to making these invaluable records freely available," said NGS President David E. Rencher, AG, CG, FUGA, FIGRS, FNGS, FSG. "We thank all who have donated to the project and to those of our partners and the many genealogical societies who spearheaded efforts to raise the funds needed, particularly the Indiana, Illinois, and Fairfax, Virginia, Genealogical Societies."

War of 1812 pensions provide information on a generation between the Revolutionary War and the 1850 census, which is the first census to provide the names of individuals in a household. The files may include an affidavit from the soldier or widow including where he enlisted, where he served, and for how long. The widow may state their date of marriage, when he died, a Bible record which may include the names and birth dates of children, and affidavits from other relatives which may help prove family relationships. Sometimes the information about the widow or an affidavit from her will disclose her maiden name. These files may also contain other meaningful military records and information on a person's fellow veterans or neighbors.

"These records are extremely valuable to researchers and historians, and we are proud to be a part of this project. We're grateful for the efforts started by the Federation of Genealogical Societies before it merged with NGS in 2020, and it has been an honor to carry this forward and continue the work with our partners to see it to completion," said NGS Executive Director Matt Menashes, CAE.

"The project serves as a template for future initiatives illustrating that together, the genealogical community can help preserve and make available important genealogical records for generations to come. These records may be used not only for genealogy, but also for those studying history and as part of a school curriculum for students," stated Rencher. "Thank you to all who made this possible!"

NGS offers an online course, War of 1812 Records, for anyone wanting a deeper understanding of how to interpret these records and what other records might add to the story. The modules guide participants through War of 1812 military records, historical context, and research strategies. More information and registration can be found on the NGS website.

Access the War of 1812 pension files via Fold3 and learn more about the project's completion on their blog.

#5363. Google acquires Seattle startup Howie and its AI scheduling assistant

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 18, 2026 at 2:03 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 2:03 pm

Google is bringing Seattle-based Howie, maker of an AI scheduling assistant that works from your inbox, into its Google Labs division.

Terms of the deal were not disclosed this week. Google Labs, the company’s experimental arm, announced the acquisition in a post on X, saying it “can’t wait to learn from them as we build the next generation of intuitive AI tools together for small businesses.”

Howie CEO and co-founder Austin Petersmith said on LinkedIn that the team will continue building Howie at Google. “Howie has always been built on top of Gmail and Google Calendar, so Google Labs is the perfect place for us to take this product to the next level,” he wrote.

Petersmith co-founded Howie around 2023 with CTO Dave Newman. The two first worked together in 2013 at Assembly, which Newman co-founded, and prototyped an AI assistant in 2015 before deciding the market wasn’t ready.

We’re excited to welcome Howie to Google Labs! The @Howie_ai team has spent years figuring out scheduling and calendar management. We can’t wait to learn from them as we build the next generation of intuitive AI tools together for small businesses 🤝 https://t.co/8bzjebeGdD

Users cc Howie on an email thread, and it coordinates meeting times, adds events to calendars, follows up as needed and flags scheduling conflicts. Customers set their own rules in an open-ended preferences document, such as “if it’s a pitch call, set it to 25 minutes and use Zoom.”

Behind the scenes, Howie ran tasks through fine-tuned language models and looped in human scheduling experts when the AI wasn’t confident.

Howie raised a $6 million seed round led by True Ventures in September 2025, when it launched publicly out of private beta. At the time, it had more than 1,000 paying customers, including startup founders, venture capitalists, recruiters, consultants and journalists, and was scheduling more than 5,000 meetings a week.

The deal comes as Google and rivals including OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta race to build AI agents that complete tasks on behalf of users. Google Labs acquired music generation platform ProducerAI earlier this year.

#5362. Zeno Power makes progress on an underwater power system that will eventually go nuclear

by Alan Boyle on Nov 19, 2026 at 7:00 amNovember 19, 2026 at 8:01 am

Zeno Power has hit a major milestone in its push to build nuclear batteries for underwater use.

The startup said today that it successfully demonstrated an electrically heated Stirling generator in a controlled maritime setting in Washington state. The two-week demonstration produced electrical power outputs in excess of 20 watts, said Lindsey Boles, Zeno’s chief product officer.

“It’s a really big step for us — just solidifying our expertise in how to design these, and then confirming our ability to translate that into operational hardware that meets or exceeds what our customers need,” Boles told GeekWire.

Zeno is developing the power system with support from the Department of Defense as a follow-up to an initial $7.5 million contract awarded in 2023. The generator uses a Stirling engine to convert heat into electricity by cycling gas through heating and cooling phases in a closed cylinder.

For the recent demonstration, the prototype device relied on an electric heating element. Future devices will instead rely on heat generated by the radioactive decay of strontium-90, a radioisotope that can be extracted from spent nuclear fuel.

Nuclear batteries have been in use for decades, primarily for space missions ranging from the Apollo moon shots to NASA’s Voyager spacecraft and Mars rovers. But the batteries being developed by Zeno Power promise to be at least four times more efficient than traditional radioisotope thermoelectric generators, Boles said.

Boles said the non-radiological test exceeded expectations. “There’s a difference between a design that works on paper and hardware that works in the field,” she said in a news release. “This is the moment our team has been building toward: proof that this technology works outside the lab.”

Long-lasting nuclear batteries could be used to power undersea sensor networks or recharge autonomous underwater vehicles. “There are a lot of applications, especially on the maritime front, that we really want electricity for,” Boles said. “And we really don’t need a ton of it. But we need it to be really reliable, and we need it to be long endurance, and we need it to be self-managed. … I think of it like a slow Tesla supercharger on the seabed.”

Retired Navy Adm. John Richardson, former chief of naval operations and a member of Zeno’s board of directors, called the recent test an “important step toward undersea superiority.”

“Protecting maritime infrastructure and powering distributed systems at sea requires energy; energy that lasts for years, not days or months,” Richardson said in a written statement. “As competition intensifies in contested domains, powered subsea systems will help keep us ahead. Zeno Power has steadily reduced risk, proven its technology, built a supply chain, and prepared to scale production.”

Next year, Zeno Power plans to install a radioisotope heat source in its generator and test the system in a water tank under controlled laboratory conditions. If those tests are successful, Zeno will move forward with the first operational seabed deployment of its radioisotope-fueled maritime system later in 2027.

The maritime battery isn’t Zeno’s only product. The company is also working on a nuclear-powered heater system for spacecraft, with a demonstration on the lunar surface planned as early as 2028. Zeno’s broader vision is to provide long-lasting, reliable power on the moon and Mars, and in extreme environments on Earth.

Since its founding in 2018, Zeno has secured $105 million in private capital and has brought in $60 million in contracts with the Pentagon and NASA. The company has more than 95 employees at locations in Seattle, California and Washington, D.C., with the largest contingent working at its engineering headquarters in Seattle’s South Lake Union district.

#5360. The U.S. is preparing to raise tariffs on China, the E.U., and 14 other countries

The U.S. Trade Representative is expected to unveil results of its industrial subsidies investigation as soon as Tuesday

Allen J. Schaben / Los Angeles Times via Getty Images

The U.S. is getting ready to hike duties on imports from China, the European Union and 14 other economies in response to their industrial subsidies, according to The Wall Street Journal.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer could announce the results of his office's investigation as soon as Tuesday, according to Bloomberg. The timing could change, according to The Wall Street Journal. Tariff rates and an effective date are unclear.

The probe falls under Section 301 of the 1974 Trade Act, a provision that lets a president act alone in levying tariffs in response to unfair trade conduct, according to Bloomberg. The Office of the U.S. Trade Representative opened the investigation in March, following the high court's invalidation of President Donald Trump's earlier worldwide tariffs.

Greer has said that state backing, subsidies among it, has left the targeted economies with more industrial production capacity than they need. He has said that this lets companies in those economies undercut competitors abroad on price, which hurts American manufacturers. The U.S. Trade Representative's office declined to comment, according to The Wall Street Journal and Bloomberg. The White House did not respond to requests for comment from The Wall Street Journal or Bloomberg.

The new tariffs are expected to apply to the bulk of goods coming from the targeted nations, among them China, Japan, South Korea and the E.U.'s 27 member states, according to The Wall Street Journal. Steel, aluminum and automobiles are expected to be left out because they are already subject to duties under another law tied to national security.

Administration officials have said they plan to set rates close to the ones Trump put in place during 2025, ahead of the Supreme Court's invalidation of his initial round of tariffs in February 2026, according to The Wall Street Journal. Countries with trade agreements, including Japan, the E.U. and South Korea, are expected to face rates of 15% or lower. Vietnam and India could be hit with steeper rates that reflect the agreements they struck with Trump.

China is expected to be charged a steeper tariff than many of its peers because Trump officials have described its subsidies as especially far-reaching, according to The Wall Street Journal. The administration could add wording that would let it increase tariffs if a country's overcapacity in industry grows worse or if the country fails to change its policies during later talks.

The new duties are expected to stack on top of tariffs announced in July over forced labor, according to The Wall Street Journal. Those tariffs, which run from 10% to 12.5% on about 60 economies, are being contested in a lawsuit before the Court of International Trade, according to Bloomberg.

#5359. Amazon’s $18B bet on Anthropic tops $200B, for a moment, in the Claude maker’s historic market debut

by Todd Bishop on Nov 19, 2026 at 9:54 amNovember 19, 2026 at 10:10 am

Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut today in a record $81.3 billion initial public offering, with big financial stakes for the Seattle area’s two tech giants.

For Amazon, the IPO is a paper windfall. The company started putting money into Anthropic in 2023, about $18 billion in all. At the $83 IPO price, its stake was worth about $161 billion. With Anthropic opening at $111.50 a share, that number was closer to $216 billion. The stock has since dropped below $100, which put Amazon’s stake under $200 billion.

Beyond the value of the investment, Anthropic is a major customer for Amazon’s cloud platform. The Claude maker has committed to spend at least $110 billion on Amazon Web Services through 2036.

For Microsoft, it’s more complicated. The Redmond company agreed in late 2025 to invest up to $5 billion but hasn’t disclosed the size of its stake. Microsoft is buying $1 billion of Anthropic stock alongside the IPO, one of seven tech companies buying a combined $26 billion. Anthropic has committed to spend at least $47 billion on Microsoft’s Azure cloud through 2033.

But Microsoft is also pitching its own AI models against Anthropic’s, and it has been working to replace Anthropic’s models with OpenAI’s in some Copilot features, The Information reported this week.

Listing Anthropic’s compute partners on CNBC this morning, co-founder Daniela Amodei named Nvidia, Amazon, Google and Broadcom, but not Microsoft. Whether it was a slip or something more significant, it was an interesting omission.

A historic debut: The offering tops SpaceX’s $75 billion IPO in June, and it makes Anthropic the first standalone AI lab to go public, ahead of OpenAI.

The five-year-old company was valued at about $1.5 trillion at the $83 IPO price, on a fully diluted basis that counts employee stock and other shares not yet issued. The stock opened at $111.50, valuing Anthropic at about $2 trillion on the same basis. It has since traded as low as about $95.

Speaking before the opening bell, CEO Dario Amodei said Anthropic will slow the training and release of its AI models for as long as it takes to be confident they’re safe, and that going public only strengthens that resolve.

“We will not bend to either business nor political pressure,” he said.

In an interview with CNBC’s Andrew Ross Sorkin afterward, Amodei called the push and pull between growth and that kind of restraint “one of the central tensions at the heart of the company.”

Anthropic is also a public benefit corporation, a structure that legally requires the company to balance shareholders’ interests with the public good.

What’s next: Both Seattle-area giants have hedged their bets. Microsoft owns about 24% of OpenAI, and Amazon put $50 billion into OpenAI earlier this year.

OpenAI, which confidentially filed for its own IPO in June, is still aiming to go public in 2027.

Anthropic’s co-founders and some of its biggest shareholders are barred from selling for up to a year under the IPO’s lock-up rules, and Amazon has said it expects a customary lock-up period.

Amazon will update the value of its Anthropic holdings in its fourth-quarter results, much of it through earnings, which means the paper windfall is likely to boost Amazon’s fourth-quarter profit even though it hasn’t sold a share.

#5357. Former xAI founders are launching a predictive AI startup called Epochal

Epochal says its time portal lets AI agents browse the internet as it existed on past dates, with trillions of pages over 30 years

Epochal, a new AI startup, announced a tool on Tuesday that gives AI agents a way to view the web as it looked on a past date.

The company was started by three of the people who founded Elon Musk's xAI and exited after he folded it into SpaceX in February, according to Bloomberg. They are Guodong Zhang, Zihang Dai and Manuel Kroiss. Former staffers from xAI, OpenAI, Anthropic and Google $GOOGL DeepMind have joined them.

Epochal calls the tool the Epochal Time Portal and said it holds trillions of pages spanning 30 years of history. The company said it believes the best measure of intelligence is the ability to predict the future, which requires learning from the past and working to be less wrong.

Epochal said current AI systems learn from the internet all at once, knowing how each story ends. It wants AI to live through thousands of yesterdays, one day at a time, the way people do.

Epochal's goal, according to Bloomberg, is a model meant to assist people when they have choices to make.

Zhang is putting $100 million into the company, according to Bloomberg, which cited an unnamed source. An Epochal spokesperson would not discuss funding, Bloomberg said.

Epochal joins a growing list of new companies founded by people who departed xAI this year, according to Bloomberg. xAI co-founder Igor Babuschkin started River AI, a personalized AI startup, alongside several ex-xAI and Tesla $TSLA employees. Former xAI staffers Yuchen He and Eric Zelikman were part of the founding team behind the AI lab Humans&.
