#5335. Startup Spotlight: An engineer’s search for better, safer baby products led him to launch Birch

Startup Spotlight profiles tech startups in the Pacific Northwest.

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 20, 2026 at 9:41 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:41 am

A new baby can be the ultimate anxiety trigger: When will she sleep through the night? What if nursing is a challenge. What is that rash?! Given the countless unknowns, the last thing a parent needs are worries about the quality of the baby’s crib or the chemicals in a pacifier.

But when Karthik Gangiredla was preparing for the birth of his first daughter, he and his wife spent hours trying to figure out which baby products were trustworthy.

“We struggled a lot,” Gangiredla said. “We did a lot of research on what was safe, what’s not.”

An engineer with roughly 20 years of experience in supply chains and logistics, including roles at Amazon, Flexport and TikTok, Gangiredla found himself on the consumer side of the retail equation, scrutinizing strollers and bottles.

To spare other parents the same headache, he turned that research into Birch, an online marketplace that offers baby product buying guides and assigns each item a TrustScore. Its scoring system draws on certifications, lab reports and recall databases to help parents assess goods ranging from baby wipes to teething toys.

The site provides information on more than 10,000 items across 110 brands, including manufacturing locations, suppliers, certificate numbers and test reports.

Birch has contracts with brands it has checked out, and serves as their merchant of record, meaning if a customer has issues with a product or wants to return it, Birch handles those steps. It operates fulfillment centers in Los Angeles and New Jersey.

Gangiredla said the startup flips the e-commerce approach of retail giants, focusing on the shoppers’ needs, not those of the merchant. It does not accept ads or sponsored rankings.

If you took away the ad revenue for Amazon or TikTok, “the business wouldn’t exist,” Gangiredla said. “So it’s very difficult for them to approach the problem in a different way.”

The platform also offers a gift registry and tools for tracking fetal development during pregnancy, an infant’s nursing and sleep schedules, and other developmental steps. The tools are free for users.

We caught up with Gangiredla, Birch’s CEO and founder, for this edition of GeekWire’s Startup Spotlight.

In 50 words or less, give us your startup’s elevator pitch

Birch is the trust-first platform for baby and kids products and parenting resources. We research and score products across 50+ safety and quality signals before listing — and stock only what clears the bar — so parents skip the endless research and buy with confidence, from pregnancy through the toddler years.

What problem are you obsessed with solving?

The impossible research burden on new parents. Every purchase feels like a safety decision, the information is scattered and often unverified, and the stakes feel enormous. We’re obsessed with moving the work of figuring out what’s trustworthy off the parent and onto a system that does it rigorously — and then showing our work.

What surprised you after talking to customers?

How universal the trust problem is. We assumed it would track with income or with first-time parents, but our customers span all 50 states and every kind of household — big metros to small towns. And what they consistently want isn’t more options or a lower price; it’s someone to tell them, credibly, what’s actually worth buying.

How has AI changed the way you build your company?

It’s core, not a feature. Our TrustScore engine evaluates thousands of products across dozens of safety and quality signals in ways a human team our size never could, and the same intelligence powers discovery and personalization. It also lets a very lean team operate like a much larger one — and we now license that engine to other baby and kids brands as a product called Juno.

What’s one thing people misunderstand about your startup?

That “curated” means limited or expensive. Curation isn’t about carrying less for its own sake, or about selling premium — it’s about removing the untrustworthy. In our own data, price and trustworthiness barely correlate; some of the highest-scoring products are among the most affordable. Fewer and better, not fewer and pricier.

What’s the toughest decision you’ve made in the past year?

Turning away brands and revenue. When you’re early, every dollar is tempting — but our entire promise is that everything on Birch has earned its place. Saying no to products and partners that didn’t clear the bar, even when the revenue was real, was hard. It’s also the decision that defines what we are.

What’s the one piece of advice you give to other entrepreneurs?

Earn trust before you try to scale it. It’s slower and less glamorous than chasing growth, but trust compounds and shortcuts don’t. And talk to your customers far earlier, and far more often, than feels comfortable.

…a parent’s first instinct, the moment they find out they’re expecting, is to come to Birch — and “did you check the TrustScore?” is just how families talk about buying for their kids.

#5334. Iraq is challenging OPEC+'s assessment of its oil production capacity

Baghdad disputes a consultants' study that put its maximum at under 5 million barrels a day ahead of Sunday's OPEC+ meeting

Iraq has turned down OPEC+'s commissioned review of how much oil it can produce, according to Bloomberg. The dispute could spark a confrontation at the group's online meeting on Sunday, Nov 29., where OPEC and its allies, under Saudi leadership, plan to rely on the findings to set production targets.

Baghdad is contesting a study by outside consultants, who put its maximum capacity at less than 5 million barrels a day, according to Bloomberg. Oil Minister Basim Mohammed Khudair has written to OPEC to insist that Iraq can reach 5.2 million barrels a day.

Under the review, a country given a bigger capacity figure has a firmer basis for seeking a larger output allowance, according to Bloomberg. Iraq's oil ministry and OPEC's secretariat in Vienna had not responded to requests for comment from Bloomberg as of its publication.

This year, Iraq warned it could exit OPEC unless the assessment credited it with a sufficiently large number, according to Bloomberg. Iraq later withdrew the warning. The warning came weeks after the United Arab Emirates' exit from the group, and the UAE has since pushed its production to record levels.

Iraq has bristled at OPEC+ quotas for 10 years, wanting to boost its earnings and restore an economy hurt by war and sanctions, according to Bloomberg.

The two sides have also differed on how much Iraq is producing. Iraq told OPEC its October output came to nearly 4.9 million barrels daily, the highest of the wartime period and far over its quota, according to Bloomberg. Figures that OPEC draws from outside sources put the number at 4.491 million barrels a day.

OPEC and its allies have been examining the volumes each member can technically produce as groundwork for 2027 output targets.

Separately, the International Energy Agency put Iraq's sustainable capacity at 4.87 million barrels a day in its monthly oil market report this month. The agency estimated Iraq's October output at 4.6 million barrels a day, the highest since September 2019.

#5333. Microsoft ‘To Do’ users make a big to-do over popular task app’s pending retirement

by Todd Bishop on Nov 20, 2026 at 2:06 pmNovember 20, 2026 at 2:07 pm

Microsoft acquired the popular Wunderlist app in 2015, shut it down in 2020 and told its loyal users that Microsoft To Do would be their new home. Now they’re being asked to pack up again.

Microsoft plans to retire the To Do apps on June 30, 2027, moving personal task management for work and school accounts into Planner, its team project-management app. Microsoft disclosed the change Wednesday in a long Planner blog post amid the company’s Ignite announcements, and Windows Latest flagged the change later that day.

The reaction was swift and mostly unhappy. Tom Warren of The Verge summed it up on X: “Microsoft is killing its great tasks app in favor of its worse tasks app.”

That’s not entirely fair to Planner, which is built for a different job. But it captures the gripe: To Do was simple, free and worked across Windows, Mac, iOS, Android and the web, and nothing Microsoft is offering replaces all of that.

For work and school accounts, Microsoft says Planner “will be the destination for managing personal work tasks,” but “existing To Do tasks and lists will not migrate to Planner.” It says it will offer a way to export To Do data before the app shuts down.

Tony Redmond of Office365itpros, who tracks Microsoft 365 closely, cataloged the gaps: no file attachments on private Planner tasks, no equivalent for To Do’s list groups, no transfer of shared-list membership, assignments or permissions, and no native Planner apps for Windows or Mac.

He also noted the irony that Outlook’s old Exchange-based tasks will outlive To Do.

Why Microsoft is doing it: The company said putting individual and shared work on the same foundation lets it deliver more consistent features, and lets people connect their own tasks to Copilot and other AI agents. A new Planner agent, available with a Copilot add-on license, can take on tasks and generate status reports.

The Register’s Richard Speed put it less charitably, saying Microsoft had slipped the news into “this week’s Ignite AI puffery.”

Users weigh in: Brad Silverberg, the former Microsoft executive who led Windows 95 development and later became a Seattle venture investor, posted on X that he has used To Do daily, and Wunderlist before it.

“Very disappointed now,” he wrote, adding that he’s looking at TickTick and Todoist.

Similar posts piled up on LinkedIn from Microsoft 365 consultants and everyday users, some of them describing Planner as clunky by comparison.

Patrick Husting, a Seattle-area entrepreneur and software developer whose Ghostwriter add-in brought AI to Microsoft Office before Microsoft announced Microsoft 365 Copilot, offered on LinkedIn to maintain To Do for Microsoft for free.

Rivals smell an opportunity: Competitors wasted no time. TickTick posted a migration guide for To Do refugees. Todoist CEO Amir Salihefendic wrote on LinkedIn that the shutdown was “pretty unexpected” and pointed out that his app has outlasted competitors for 20 years.

The most pointed pitch came from Superlist, which called itself “the natural successor” and said it already has a tool for importing To Do lists. Wunderlist founder Christian Reber started the company in 2020.

Reber and his co-founders sold Wunderlist’s parent company, 6Wunderkinder, to Microsoft in 2015 for a reported $100 million to $200 million. In 2019, as Microsoft prepared to shut the app down, he publicly asked Satya Nadella to sell it back. Microsoft kept it, then retired it in favor of To Do.

Now some of those former Wunderlist users may end up back with the people who built it.

#5332. Nvidia degrades U.S. national security as Chinese military snags its chips

When Super Micro compliance auditors visited a Southeast Asian customer in August 2025 to inspect thousands of servers packed with Nvidia chips, the warehouse floor looked in order. According to federal prosecutors, the scene was pure theater. The servers on hand were nonworking dummies staged for the audit; the real ones had already gone to China. When Commerce Department inspectors came later, conspirators set up the same fakes again, using a hair dryer to swap labels and serial stickers. Prosecutors say at least $510 million in servers went to China over a few weeks in spring 2025 alone.

Fifteen months later, the country is once again being asked to take tidy paperwork at face value. In less than two weeks, Nvidia’s leadership turmoil swung through an astonishing reversal. Jensen Huang abruptly resigned as chief executive on November 12, and five days later the company’s chairman declared that the board “does not intend to reinstate” him. Come Monday, directors brought him back anyway, citing assurances from senior U.S. officials and concluding that his return “poses no national security risk.” President Donald Trump claimed credit for talking them into it, telling CNBC, “It’s a threat to lose him.”

Official endorsements cannot wish away the serious security record piling up in the public view. Set aside, for a moment, the scrutiny swirling around Megaspeed, the firm tied to Huang’s paramour Alice Huang, as well as the question of whether she acted as a spy. Even apart from that controversy, a largely overlooked trove of documentation proves beyond dispute that restricted and banned Nvidia chips have been illegally shipped into China, where the Chinese military has openly recorded buying elite processors to bolster capabilities aimed against the United States.

Congressional investigators, state attorneys general, and the broader national security community will inevitably unravel what transpired with Megaspeed and Alice Huang. As they pursue that thread, however, they cannot lose sight of the larger pipeline operating right under Washington’s nose. Smuggled American chips are already strengthening the Chinese Communist Party’s military power and domestic repression, fueling weapons research, design, and manufacturing alongside electronic warfare and intelligence collection. Before anyone treats Huang’s return as case closed, investigators must confront the pressing, unanswered questions still hanging over Nvidia.

Consider some of the military-linked recipients already plainly visible in public records. A Reuters investigation published November 11 found that Northwestern Polytechnical University, a military-linked institution on the U.S. export blacklist since 2001 over alleged missile proliferation, recorded an October purchase of two H200 chips through a Chinese supplier. Its cybersecurity school also contracted in January for access to two servers containing eight H200s apiece.

Some advocates point out that the H200 is an older and less sensitive chip, but the administration’s January H200 licensing relaxation explicitly did not erase restrictions on blacklisted entities. Indeed, its safeguards expressly excluded military and military-intelligence users and prohibited remote access for specified restricted parties. The university’s disturbing procurement records therefore demand a detailed explanation: what authorization, if any, covered these supplies, and which intermediary checked the actual beneficiary? Did the U.S. government authorize these sales (it would be ludicrously stupid if so), or did Nvidia fail in its responsibility to monitor its own supply chain and maintain awareness of end customers?

The Harbin Institute of Technology offers another disturbing example. When Commerce blacklisted it in 2020, the department specifically cited efforts to acquire American technology for Chinese missile programs. Yet Reuters reported this March that Harbin’s July 2025 procurement notice described a Super Micro system containing eight Nvidia A100s. Beihang University, another blacklisted institution with military ties, recorded purchasing a workstation with four A100s in March 2026.

At a minimum, all of this points to persistent demand from the Chinese military and institutions linked to it — the very institutions the controls were designed to exclude and the very institutions that want to hurt U.S. national security the most. Who is dropping the ball here?

If the Chinese military has its way, more banned Nvidia chips will soon be on their way. WireScreen reviewed more than 3,800 Chinese military and government procurement records. The units seeking Nvidia hardware include the Rocket Force, which operates China’s land-based nuclear missiles, the Cyberspace Force, and the equipment arm of the Communist Party’s Central Military Commission. One Cyberspace Force tender for A100-class servers named a password-cracking tool as the workload. Georgetown researchers found a PLA lab requesting 16 H100s and another unit seeking a DeepSeek-linked cyber range for “intelligent attack.”  That should scare any and every American.

It is not just the Chinese military obtaining older, still-restricted Nvidia chips. There is also ample evidence that the most cutting-edge, most sensitive chips—such as the Blackwell chip, which is entirely banned from being sold into China—are still making their way into China anyway, and worse, directly into the hands of the CCP. Last month, the AI security firm Lava reported finding 32 NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra B300 GPUs operating on Chinese networks—specifically linked to state-owned China Telecom—during a study of more than 12,000 GPUs, despite a ban on Blackwell chips going to China. That comes on top of the fact that even a senior administration official says DeepSeek trained a model on banned Blackwell chips, likely in Inner Mongolia. Congressional investigators should demand answers about how these Blackwell chips are getting into China and whether Nvidia is asleep at the switch on the most basic KYC duties—know your customer.

Nvidia surely must know about the transshipment of its sensitive chips into China – as has already been proven in the public record, with a long trail of criminal indictments. Alan Hao Hsu and his company, Hao Global, pleaded guilty in October 2025. According to the Justice Department, the scheme involved at least $160 million in exported and attempted exports of restricted Nvidia H100 and H200 processors. Shipping documents concealed the goods and recipients; more than $50 million in funding originated in China. The company’s plea agreement identifies transshipment through Singapore and Malaysia. This is admitted criminal conduct involving falsified documentation and illegal exports through transshipments, yet what did Nvidia do about the facilitators of that transshipment who were still getting chips from Nvidia?

Similarly, in March, federal prosecutors alleged that defendants connected to Super Micro arranged purchases through a Southeast Asian intermediary and diverted at least $510 million in servers to China within weeks in spring 2025, then used the dummy servers described at the outset to cover their tracks. In October, broker Ting-Wei Sun pleaded guilty to four counts, including export-control conspiracy and obstruction. Similarly, Taiwan has indicted a senior Nvidia manager as the central figure in faking a compliance audit so that 74 servers of top-line B300 chips could reach China. Given these apparent leaks and holes across Nvidia’s supply chain, any reasonable observer would conclude the company needs to monitor its own customers and employees far more carefully.

Whenever Washington weighs a firmer line on chips, the same warning reliably surfaces. Push Beijing too hard, skeptics caution, and China will choke off the rare earth magnets powering everything from fighter jets to electric motors. That anxiety is already dictating policy. After the administration let Nvidia resume H20 sales to China last year, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick was candid about the bargain, explaining, “We put that in the trade deal with the magnets.” Export controls once considered untouchable have stayed on the bargaining table ever since.

Beijing’s current leverage is undeniable. According to the International Energy Agency, China mines roughly 60% of the world’s magnet rare earths, refines around 90%, and makes nearly 95% of finished permanent magnets. Its grip tightens further on heavy rare earths like dysprosium and terbium, which keep magnets working at high temperatures inside military hardware and electric vehicle motors. Benchmark Mineral Intelligence found that as recently as 2024, the West depended on China for 99% of those heavy minerals. Nor has Beijing hesitated to flex that advantage. Export controls imposed in April 2025 on seven heavy rare earths remain in force. In June, China blacklisted two American firms championed by federal policymakers, MP Materials and USA Rare Earth, and this month it extended a pause on broader restrictions by just two months.

Their dominance, however, is a product of policy rather than geology, and it can erode far faster than conventional wisdom expects. Rare earths are not actually rare. All 17 occur outside China, and the U.S. Geological Survey estimates that more than 40 percent of reported global reserves—and an even larger share of identified deposits—lie beyond China’s borders, including 11 million metric tons in Brazil alone, along with major deposits across Australia, Canada, Greenland, Tanzania, and the United States. As late as the 1980s, the world’s leading producer was not in Asia at all, but a single mine in California’s Mojave Desert called Mountain Pass. China assembled its commanding lead in roughly twenty years.

Japan has already demonstrated how swiftly the balance can shift. After Beijing halted exports to Japan in 2010, Tokyo bankrolled Australia’s Lynas and cut China’s share of Japanese rare earth imports from over 90% to roughly 60% within a decade. Lynas has since become the first producer outside China capable of separating both dysprosium and terbium.

The true bottleneck is not ore, but processing capacity and permits, both of which can be solved in years instead of decades. While the IEA estimates that meeting demand for magnet rare earths outside China will require roughly $60 billion over the next ten years, the figure is a modest fraction of the $1.2 trillion in U.S. economic activity Bloomberg calculates depends on these materials. Washington has begun laying the groundwork, pairing a Pentagon stake and price floor for MP Materials with the $12 billion Project Vault stockpile and $565 million for Brazil’s Serra Verde, which supplies those same vital heavy rare earths.

Permitting remains the stubborn obstacle. S&P Global calculates that taking a new American mine from discovery to production averages 29 years, slower than every country on earth except Zambia and almost ten years behind Australia. Delays on such a scale turn responsible oversight into outright paralysis. Clearing the logjam demands an “Operation Warp Speed” for critical minerals, built on hard permitting deadlines, one lead agency per project, guaranteed offtake for allied producers stretching from Brazil and Canada to Africa, and strict environmental standards enforced upfront without endless litigation. Smart environmental policy is essential, yet reflexive obstruction simply ships both the mining and the pollution straight to China.

Beijing’s rare earth card is a wasting asset, provided Washington chooses to make it one. The answer is to build, not to bend, and certainly not to keep weakening the export controls standing between America’s best technology and the People’s Liberation Army.

Congress holds subpoena power, and they ought to wield it to get to the bottom of how the Chinese military is obtaining banned Nvidia chips. Nvidia’s shipment ledger for every GPU sent to Southeast Asia since October 2022 is fair game and in the company’s possession, as are any location data its fleet-management software has collected, its customer files and communication with US regulators, including the Department of Commerce.

State attorneys general are paving the way, as California Attorney General Rob Bonta has already subpoenaed Nvidia on how chips reached China and whether investors were misled.

Export controls were meant to keep America’s best chips out of China’s war machine, yet the evidence shows that Nvidia’s most sensitive chips are already fueling the Chinese military in its quest to degrade US national security. The only crime greater than smuggling these chips into the hands of the Chinese military would be our neglect in letting them get away with it.

As the line often attributed to Lenin goes, “Capitalists will sell you the rope used to hang them.”

#5331. The Counterintuitive Sales Strategy That Built My Business

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

I used to carry a seven-figure sales quota working for a large consulting firm. Selling as a solopreneur is a totally different game — but I like it much more.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

By all accounts, I was a phenomenal salesperson. I always exceeded my quota, which in the sales world meant that my quota increased every year. But just because I was effective doesn’t mean that I loved it.

When you’re selling inside a large organization with a seven-figure quota, there are things you simply have to do to hit your numbers. For me, that meant pushing and pitching to just about anyone who would listen, and it took a heavy toll on my mental health.

The toll came from feeling that I had to do things that didn’t align with my ethics or my entrepreneurial beliefs. In the seven years I’ve run my agency, I haven’t had to compromise my ethics to build a book of business or grow my pipeline. Instead, I’ve focused on what I call selling by helping.

Rather than pushing and pitching at every opportunity, I found places where my ideal clients were raising their hands and asking for help, and I simply offered to help them. Only a small fraction of the people I’ve helped have ended up needing my service. But the ones who did were exactly the people my business was built to serve, and the ones who got the most value from it.

As AI makes sales outreach more automated, I believe this human approach will matter more than ever. Here’s how to put it into practice — and the tool I’d recommend to support it.

However advanced AI gets, buyers will still want to deal with real humans. A recent study conducted by HubSpot and SurveyMonkey found that 82% of consumers prefer human support, even when outcomes and wait times are the same. Trust is built through relationships, and relationships are ultimately rooted in human connection. Even before AI, plenty of companies failed to make selling feel human.

That was the part of the sales profession I disliked most — and the part I resisted when I was selling full-time. It’s also why selling by helping is the opposite of the impersonal approach so common in modern sales. The RAIN Group Center for Sales Research found that 96% of buyers say a seller’s focus on the value they can deliver influences their purchase decision. Furthermore, 90% of organizations classified as value-driven experienced year-over-year revenue growth, compared to 72% of organizations that weren’t value-driven.

As you have more conversations focused on genuinely helping someone, resist the urge to turn your help into a quid pro quo. Lead with value instead of trying to extract it. When you do, what comes back to you is worth far more than anything you could have extracted.

In practice, that means knowing when to end the conversation. Imagine you’ve just had a great conversation with someone who looks like an ideal client, and you’ve really helped them. In a traditional sales environment, that’s when you’d pitch. With selling by helping, you end the conversation once you’ve added value. No chasing, no pitching and no pushing anyone toward a sale.

That doesn’t mean you forget about them. Remember who they are, build a natural connection and stay in touch, always by adding value. The payoff is that when they need the service you offer, you’ll be top of mind. At least, that has been my experience. That’s how you sell like a human.

My company works in the Salesforce ecosystem and has a free app on the AppExchange, so we have Salesforce licenses in-house. But I use a CRM far less than I did when I was selling full-time. When you’re leading with value, it doesn’t matter whether you track relationships in a CRM, an Excel sheet or a notebook. The tool won’t change your approach to selling.

The one place I have found worth investing in is LinkedIn. I tell the founders I coach that they don’t need a website to launch a solo agency. They need a LinkedIn presence that makes it obvious who they help and how.

That’s where LinkedIn Premium Business comes in. It lets you showcase what you offer on your own service page, share client testimonials and collect reviews as you build your business. It also fits naturally with my selling-by-helping methodology. You can connect directly with your ideal customers, and Advice Sessions let you offer one-on-one help right from your LinkedIn profile, so leading with value becomes part of how you do business.

Not all of your business will come through LinkedIn, but that’s one more reason to get your presence right. Whenever I help someone in a public forum, the next thing I do is connect with them on LinkedIn, always with a personalized note, so the relationship starts naturally. From there, I can stay in touch, and my ideal clients can see the content I create and share.

That content should lead with value, too. Teach, share what you’re learning and answer the questions your ideal clients are already asking. Then, when they’re ready for a transformation of their own, you’ll be the first person they think to call.

LinkedIn Premium Business can also help you get that content in front of more of your ideal clients, expanding your network and boosting your visibility, while embracing my selling-by-helping methodology at every touchpoint.

If you’re ready to start selling by helping, LinkedIn’s new Small Business Playbook offers practical ways to build your brand, grow your network and find customers. You can also explore LinkedIn’s tools for small businesses to find the ones that fit how you work.

#5330. AEREDIUM bets parallel execution can raise blockchain speed limits

Most blockchains process transactions one at a time. AEREDIUM is testing whether running engines in parallel across regions can lift that limit.

This article has been reviewed by the Quartz editorial team. The content may be licensed for reuse.

Blockchain developers have long struggled to process high transaction volumes without slowing down network agreement. As digital payment systems expand, developers are exploring parallel processing to increase capacity across separate locations. According to researchers at the Bank for International Settlements, the trade-off among a blockchain's transaction capacity, the concentration of its stakeholders, and its security is known as Buterin's scalability trilemma. Because traditional blockchains process transactions sequentially, high demand often triggers severe congestion and rising user fees during peak market activity.

Increasing speed on a traditional blockchain is far harder than upgrading standard corporate servers. In conventional computing, engineers simply add faster processors inside a single data center to handle heavier workloads. Yet distributed ledgers require independent computers across distant regions to verify every transfer and agree on a single shared history.

To address these constraints, Layer 1 blockchain AEREDIUM is testing a horizontal scaling model that runs multiple execution engines simultaneously. Rather than relying on a single processing environment, the architecture distributes transaction execution across separate geographic regions. During a Nov. 22 demonstration on its public test network, AEREDIUM reported deploying two execution engines roughly 4,000 kilometers apart. According to the company, each engine handled approximately 200,000 transactions per second during the trial.

Over a 10-second window, AEREDIUM reported processing 3 million individually signed transfers from 1,200 funded accounts, averaging roughly 300,000 transactions per second. The company said each transaction entered through the network's standard interface, completed execution and finalization, and incurred the applicable network fee. At its peak single second, the network finalized 41 full blocks of 10,000 transactions each, reaching 410,000 transactions per second. “We have now demonstrated 410,000 transactions in a single second across 41 full blocks, with every block recorded and available for public inspection,” said Albert Dadon, founder and CEO of AEREDIUM.

Instead of traditional energy-intensive mining or token-staking consensus, AEREDIUM uses an approach it calls Proof of Attestation. Under this design, attested software validates transactions inside isolated hardware enclaves to achieve single-block finality without waiting for multiple confirmation blocks. According to the National Institute of Standards and Technology, a trusted execution environment is “an area or enclave protected by a system processor.” AEREDIUM states that combining hardware-backed verification with parallel engines allows capacity to grow as new engines are added.

Still, controlled benchmarks do not automatically guarantee identical performance under continuous commercial traffic. Peak bursts of 410,000 transactions per second demonstrate short-term capacity rather than sustained output over months of complex smart-contract activity. Relying on hardware-enforced enclaves also introduces specific dependencies on processor integrity, firmware security, and reliable attestation mechanisms. Independent evaluations of larger, multi-region deployments will be necessary to confirm how well coordination holds up under heavy congestion or unexpected network outages.

Looking ahead, high-throughput parallel architectures could eventually support institutional settlement, cross-border payments, and automated trading platforms. In a June 2026 economic report, the Bank for International Settlements warned that as blockchain networks proliferate, “the benefits of scalability and efficiency are often undermined by the absence of cohesion among these frameworks.” For AEREDIUM, the long-term objective is expanding network capacity incrementally by adding regional execution engines rather than capping throughput at a fixed limit.

Ultimately, the broader significance of horizontal blockchain execution lies in shifting how developers think about network limits. Rather than treating transaction speed as a rigid ceiling, distributed execution explores whether capacity can expand alongside infrastructure demand. “Our architecture is designed to increase capacity as more execution engines are added, rather than operate toward a fixed transaction ceiling,” Dadon said. Whether parallel execution can preserve security and decentralization at global scale remains the defining test for next-generation financial networks.

#5329. CEO of $21 billion Cerebras says it’s minted 1,000 employees into millionaires—but warns that drastic changes in fortunes can be ‘really stressful’

Employees at some of the largest tech companies are scoring big thanks to stock purchase benefits. Cerebras CEO Andrew Feldman says he’s proud that his $21.7 billion AI company has turned over a thousand of its staffers into millionaires. But he knows firsthand how quickly those fortunes can change—and says employees shouldn’t get too caught up in watching their net worth yo-yo.

“What we’ve done with our team first, we made more than a thousand millionaires,” Feldman recently said on the Sourcery With Molly O’Shea channel. “That’s something I’m really proud of. I think that’s our job as leaders, to make our guys wealthy. We talked about the fact that we’re not in this for the short run, that the daily fluctuations are not what they should watch.”

As tech companies rule the U.S. stock market, all it takes is a bad earnings report or a shift in investor sentiment to send company shares on a roller-coaster ride.

Now founders and employees alike can watch their fortunes fluctuate in the span of one day. Eligible employees at Cerebras can buy company stock directly through deductions from their paychecks at a potential 15% discount, according to the company’s 2026 employee stock purchase plan (ESPP). In May, Cerebras had a standout IPO offering 30 million Class A shares at price of $185 per share, raising $5.55 billion.

Feldman’s share was estimated to be worth about $3.2 billion following the IPO, but the CEO warned workers against watching their wealth swing at the whim of the stock market.

“Change is stressful. And the vast changes in your personal wealth, both up and down, are really stressful. It’s further made challenging by the fact that your wealth is fluctuating every day—and sometimes intraday,” Feldman continued. “You try and teach people that these fluctuations that we have no control of, can’t be watched.”

Fortune reached out to Cerebras for comment.

Feldman understands how wealth can change on a dime all too well.

As the cofounder of both Cerebras and SeaMicro with previous stints at Advanced Micro Devices (AMD), Force10 Networks, and Riverstone Networks, he’s seen how stock prices fluctuate in scaling tech companies.

The CEO recalled that while working for a different business, the stock would swing up and down, impacting his equity. Within one day, his personal wealth changed more than his father had made in his entire lifetime, Feldman said.

“For a while my dad called me every day and said, ‘Why is your stock down?’ Like, ‘Dad, that’s not helpful. Come on, Dad. I know it’s down, but I don’t know why,’” Feldman continued during the podcast. “You have to modulate when it’s up—your psyche—and you’ve got to modulate when it’s down. And you’ve got to think about what your job is every day.”

To help employees navigate the pressure of wealth, Feldman has some advice for workers who find themselves sitting on a chunk of company stock.

While workers may hold on to their company stock to capitalize on future gains—or out of perceived loyalty to their employer—they shouldn’t be afraid to diversify, the Cerebras CEO advised.

“Most companies now, especially ones that have been around for years, have a way for, as a private company, for you to sell a little bit and pay yourself,” Feldman told Molly O’Shea. “There’s no reason for you to have 99% of your wealth in one stock. Professional investors don’t do it, and Mr. Employee, there’s no reason for you to do it either. I think it’s okay to sell a little bit.”

He continued, “It’s not a statement on the company, it’s a statement that your situation is such that it’s unwise to have 99% of your wealth or 95% of your wealth in a single company.”

Feldman added that there’s no pressure to make moves when a worker gets a big cash gain. People may come out of the woodwork and offer financial advice for a fee, he said, but employees can always put their wealth in a money market account and take a breather. Once they get comfortable with their situation, professionals can revisit other investment strategies. These moments of wealth also force perspective on what they want to do with their newfound coin.

“What did I do the first time we sold the company? I paid off the house. That felt good,” Feldman explained. “I think it forces you to confront some of your values. How much you’d like to give to charity, if any? Are you the type of person that wants a super flashy car?”

More than anything, Feldman believes that people should make their wealth work for them. With more money comes greater responsibilities—but the billionaire says it shouldn’t take the joy out of financial success.

“Once you have some cash, it’s okay to do nothing with it. And it’s designed so that you shouldn’t be more stressed. And certainly I’ve seen it have that impact on people when they got really really stressed,” Feldman said. “It should make your life better, rather than worse.”

#5328. Microsoft’s final Outlook outage report details testing gaps and safeguards that backfired

by Todd Bishop on Nov 21, 2026 at 9:31 amNovember 21, 2026 at 9:50 am

The bug behind last week’s global Microsoft 365 outage struck only newer, more powerful servers in a key part of Microsoft’s network. That’s because it created a kind of traffic jam inside each server, and the more work a machine tried to do at once, the worse the jam got. The newer servers are built to do more at once, so they’re the ones that seized up.

One reason Microsoft didn’t catch it in advance: it was testing on older servers.

“Our testing did not adequately represent the combination of hardware and traffic mix encountered during this incident,” the company acknowledged in its final report, released Friday evening, a week after resolving the outage that crippled Outlook and cut off email for people around the world.

Testing that more closely replicates the company’s production environment is one of 13 next steps in the report — measures the company says it will take to keep it from happening again. The list is also aimed at reassuring the businesses that rely on Microsoft for email and collaboration, after CEO Satya Nadella acknowledged at the company’s Ignite conference this week that it has work to do on resilience.

Many of the other steps identified in the report go after a bigger problem: during the incident, the safeguards meant to contain the failure spread it around the world instead.

What set it off: As detailed in Microsoft’s preliminary report last weekend, the bug at the center of the outage had been sitting dormant since July, when Microsoft started rolling out the software update that introduced it. For more than three months, it caused no problems.

The bug affected the servers that make up what Microsoft calls its network gateway, a front door that connects people to Outlook email and other Microsoft 365 services. The flaw came from a Windows update used only on those servers. Standard versions of Windows weren’t affected.

So what was the bug? Microsoft’s final report gives a partial answer, saying it came from a change to how the gateway servers handle incoming connections.

Under heavy load, it turned out, the Windows process that sets up those connections bogged down, with tasks stuck waiting on each other until the servers ran out of computing power and memory and stopped responding.

The final report doesn’t say what the July update was meant to fix. But it does lay out three conditions that finally set the bug off. Without the bug, even all three together would have been routine, the report says.

First, nearly 14% of the gateway’s server capacity was already offline that day for routine software updates. That’s normally not a problem, because Microsoft keeps enough spare capacity to absorb it. But it meant fewer servers were available to carry the load.

That’s a different explanation from the preliminary report, which blamed the missing capacity on an unrelated problem.

Second, all of Microsoft Teams’ traffic landed on those same servers. Teams normally runs through a separate gateway of its own. About 15 hours before the outage, a routing glitch on that Teams gateway in Microsoft’s US East region set off an automatic switch that moved all Teams traffic worldwide onto the servers that handle email.

Third, the U.S. workday got going. Widespread failures began around 8 a.m. Pacific, as traffic in North America climbed toward its daily peak.

How it spread: As servers stopped responding, Microsoft’s systems automatically moved their traffic to healthy servers nearby, which had the same bug and buckled under the extra load. At the low point, more than 80% of the gateway’s servers in North America were unresponsive.

The system then shifted traffic to other regions, spreading the problem further.

“Within about two hours of the broad failures that began in North America, servers in every region were affected globally,” the report says.

The preliminary report had blamed that spread partly on “a separate issue.” The final report doesn’t repeat or explain that phrase. Instead, its findings say the way Microsoft distributes traffic “can cascade failures to other regions.”

Once the servers went down, getting them back up was its own problem. As servers came back online, they were swamped by pent-up demand and froze again, a pattern engineers call a “thundering herd.” Microsoft says it will ease traffic back onto recovering servers gradually. That fix doesn’t have a date yet.

The fixes: To keep a failure from spreading again, Microsoft says it will change how its systems shift traffic between regions, so a problem in one part of the world stays there.

It also plans to split up the servers that handle email, so a surge from another service like Teams can’t take them down. And Teams will switch over only in the region that has the problem, not worldwide.

Some of the fixes are due by the end of the year, others by the end of March. Several don’t have a date yet.

Microsoft says its first notice to customers went out about 20 minutes after the outage took hold, and it plans to shorten that by the end of the year. No business email was lost, according to the report, though some delayed messages to consumer mailboxes that had been inactive for more than 30 days bounced back to senders.

The report also confirms what Microsoft said the day after the outage began: it wasn’t hackers, and it wasn’t AI. “This incident was confirmed not to be caused by a cyberattack, and we found no evidence of malicious activity,” it says. “This change was not caused by AI tooling.”

The new testing is supposed to be in place by the end of March, according to the final report. This time, the company says, the machines in the lab will actually match the ones running the service in production.

#5325. Thanksgiving closure and Black Friday early close: 2026 stock market hours

Stock market hours for Thanksgiving 2026 include a full closure and a Black Friday early close, plus Christmas dates, regular Nasdaq hours and extended sessions

Thanksgiving week 2026 squeezes the U.S. stock trading calendar into a shorter stretch than usual. Nasdaq $NDAQ's 2026 holiday schedule lists the market as closed on Thursday, November 26. It then shows an early close at 1:00 p.m. on Friday, November 27, the day widely known as Black Friday. Anyone checking stock market hours for Thanksgiving 2026 needs both dates in view.

A normal session on the Nasdaq Stock Market runs Monday through Friday, from 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. Eastern Time. A full closure removes that session entirely. An early close trims the day, and the schedule lists 1:00 p.m. as the cutoff on the affected dates.

Those changes matter for anyone who places orders, sets price alerts or plans trades around the closing bell. An order meant for the last hour of a normal day may need different timing on a shortened one. Alerts and standing instructions tied to a 4:00 p.m. finish may need adjusting too.

December brings a second set of changes. Nasdaq's schedule lists another 1:00 p.m. early close on Thursday, December 24, followed by a full closure on Friday, December 25. Christmas Day is the final entry in Nasdaq's 2026 table. Earlier in the year, the same schedule lists Labor Day, September 7, 2026, as a closure. It is the last holiday on that list before Thanksgiving.

Holiday dates are only part of the picture. Nasdaq also publishes hours for pre-market and after-hours sessions, and some of its options venues trade until 4:15 p.m. Eastern Time. Extended-hours trading comes with thinner participation and bigger price swings, and access varies by broker.

This guide covers a selection of dates and hours from Nasdaq's published schedule, not every entry in it. The slides that follow explain the Thanksgiving closure, the shortened Black Friday session, the Christmas Eve and Christmas Day changes, the regular trading day and the extended sessions. Nasdaq offers downloadable trading calendars for 2026 and 2027, along with links to its Nordic and Nasdaq Canada schedules.

The U.S. stock market is closed all day on Thursday, November 26, 2026, for Thanksgiving. Nasdaq $NDAQ lists the date as a full closure on its 2026 U.S. stock market holiday schedule. No regular trading session runs that day.

A full closure is different from a shortened day. No session is scheduled to open, and none is scheduled to close. The date drops out of the trading calendar entirely.

Timing matters for anyone who planned to act on Thursday. An order intended for the holiday has to be placed during an earlier session or held until trading resumes. Investors who rebalance on a fixed schedule or track a position into the close can account for the missing day ahead of time.

The holiday extends beyond stock exchanges. The Federal Reserve System includes Thanksgiving Day on its list of observed holidays.

On Nasdaq's 2026 calendar, the closure listed immediately before Thanksgiving is Labor Day, Monday, September 7, 2026. No other holiday sits between those two dates on the schedule.

Investors who want the dates saved can download Nasdaq's 2026 trading calendar from the same schedule page. The 2026 schedule on that page covers U.S. markets. Nasdaq links separately to holiday schedules for its Nordic markets and for Nasdaq Canada.

Nasdaq $NDAQ's 2026 holiday schedule lists Friday, November 27, 2026, as an early close, with trading ending at 1:00 p.m. The market opens that day, but the session is shorter than a normal one.

That Friday follows Thanksgiving Day, Thursday, November 26, 2026, when the market stays closed. Investors returning from the holiday get one abbreviated session before the weekend.

The early close changes the trading window, not the trading date. November 27 still counts as a market day. Anyone who usually acts late in the session has less time to do it.

The schedule's entry for November 27 gives the 1:00 p.m. time without naming a time zone. Readers should confirm with their broker which time zone applies and what the local equivalent is, rather than assume it.

Anyone planning to place, change or cancel orders that Friday should ask their broker how it handles the shortened day. That check can cover whether pre-market or after-hours trading is offered on November 27. It can also cover when Nasdaq's options venues stop trading that day.

The stock market closes early at 1:00 p.m. on Thursday, December 24, 2026, and stays shut all day on Friday, December 25, 2026, for Christmas Day. Both dates appear on Nasdaq $NDAQ's 2026 U.S. stock market holiday schedule.

Christmas Eve brings a shortened session rather than a day off. Trading opens as usual, then stops at the 1:00 p.m. cutoff listed for that date. The cutoff removes the late afternoon that a normal weekday session would include.

The schedule leaves some questions about December 24 open. It does not say whether pre-market and after-hours sessions run that day. It also does not give closing times for Nasdaq's options venues on early-close dates. Anyone planning trades in those sessions should check how their broker handles the day.

Christmas Day is a full closure, with no regular trading session at all. In 2026, December 26 and 27 fall on a Saturday and a Sunday. The Nasdaq Stock Market's regular hours run Monday through Friday only. That leaves three consecutive days without a regular session, from Friday through Sunday. Monday, December 28, does not appear on the holiday table.

Christmas Day also matters for some investment funds whose business days follow the market calendar. One fund's supplement describes its business days as those when both the New York Stock Exchange and the Federal Reserve Bank of New York are open. The same filing lists Christmas Day among the holidays when the fund is closed. The filing also treats weekends as non-operating days for both institutions.

Christmas Day is the last entry in Nasdaq's 2026 holiday table. Investors planning further ahead can download a 2027 trading calendar from the same page.

The Nasdaq $NDAQ Stock Market trades Monday through Friday from 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. Eastern Time. Six Nasdaq options venues keep trading until 4:15 p.m. ET, later than the stock market's closing bell.

That regular stock session lasts six and a half hours each weekday. It is the baseline for every date on Nasdaq's 2026 holiday schedule. The Thanksgiving, Black Friday, Christmas Eve and Christmas Day changes all alter this window.

The six options venues with the later close are Nasdaq PHLX, The Nasdaq Options Market (NOM), Nasdaq ISE, Nasdaq GEMX, Nasdaq Texas Options and Nasdaq MRX. Each one trades from 9:30 a.m. to 4:15 p.m. ET on a regular day. Options trading on these markets continues for a quarter of an hour after the main stock session ends.

Two other Nasdaq equities venues follow the same clock as the main market. Nasdaq Texas (NTX) equities and Nasdaq PSX both trade from 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. ET. Their sessions open and close alongside the Nasdaq Stock Market, without the extra time the options venues get.

Trading hours are not the same as system hours. Nasdaq lists a separate system window for each venue. Those windows are wider than the regular trading session, and they differ from one venue to the next.

The Nasdaq Stock Market system runs from 4:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. ET, a span of 16 hours. Nasdaq Texas (NTX) runs from 7:00 a.m. to 7:00 p.m. ET, a 12-hour window. Nasdaq PSX runs from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. ET, or nine hours. Nasdaq PHLX and the options markets run from 7:30 a.m. to 5:15 p.m. ET, a span of nine hours and 45 minutes.

Every one of those system windows opens before 9:30 a.m. ET and closes after 4:00 p.m. ET. Investors who need to know exactly when an order can execute on a given venue, including during shortened holiday sessions, can confirm the details with their broker.

Nasdaq $NDAQ's pre-market session runs from 4:00 a.m. to 9:30 a.m. ET, and its after-hours session runs from 4:00 p.m. to 8:00 p.m. ET. Both windows fall outside the regular weekday session.

The sessions connect directly to the regular day. Pre-market trading ends at 9:30 a.m. ET, the moment the regular session opens. After-hours trading begins at 4:00 p.m. ET, the moment it closes.

Together, the two windows add nine and a half hours to a normal weekday. The pre-market stretch lasts five and a half hours. The after-hours stretch lasts four. The regular session between them runs six and a half hours.

Those times describe Nasdaq's own sessions, not what every investor can reach. Nasdaq notes that some brokers set different hours for extended trading. It also notes that not every online broker offers extended-hours trading at all. Anyone who wants to place orders before the opening bell or after the close should confirm both points with their brokerage first.

Trading conditions also differ outside regular hours. Nasdaq warns that extended sessions carry lower liquidity, which means fewer participants are buying and selling. It also warns of higher volatility, with prices liable to swing more widely than during the regular day.

Holiday weeks add another variable. Nasdaq's 2026 schedule lists Thanksgiving Day, November 26, and Christmas Day, December 25, as full closures, with no regular session on either date. It lists Friday, November 27, and Thursday, December 24, as early closes at 1:00 p.m.

The schedule does not say whether pre-market or after-hours trading takes place on those two shortened days, or at what times. Investors who plan to trade outside regular hours on November 27 or December 24 should ask their broker how those sessions will be handled.

#5324. After the Outlook outage: Mary Jo Foley on Ignite, Microsoft’s AI pitch, and a new approach to the press

by Todd Bishop on Nov 21, 2026 at 10:09 amNovember 21, 2026 at 10:13 am

This week on the GeekWire Podcast, longtime Microsoft beat reporter Mary Jo Foley, a GeekWire contributing writer, sizes up where the company stands after one of its most eventful weeks in years.

Microsoft opened its Ignite conference with an apology for the global Outlook outage, then took direct aim at OpenAI and Anthropic on price, even though it invests in both and sells their models. We discuss the lasting damage from the outage, why enterprise customers have few places to go even when they’re fed up, and Microsoft’s pitch to make Copilot the “OS for work,” as Anthropic goes public.

Mary Jo also explains how Microsoft changed the way it rolls out news at its big conferences, what got lost along the way, and what that says about the company after the shakeup of its communications team. Plus, we weigh who from Microsoft could lead Nvidia, and the GeekWire trivia challenge goes back to 1997.

#5323. Silicon Valley divorce lawyers see surge of CEO requests for prenups and partner NDAs after the Nvidia scandal

Silicon Valley divorce lawyers are seeing surge in outreach from CEOs, founders, and high-net-worth employees who are citing the Nvidia scandal as the reason for their calls.

The revelation of Jensen Huang’s affairs, and Nvidia’s board subsequently firing him from the company he founded, is a “precautionary tale for other CEOs,” said one lawyer who has been involved in the high-profile divorces of some of the tech industry’s most famous CEOs.

Although Huang’s board reinstated him on Monday in a controversial move, the roller coaster of events has pushed other CEOs to think about how their assets are connected, and potentially at risk, as a result of their personal relationships. In addition to pursuing prenuptial agreements, many are interested in drafting nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) for their significant others, which is a new trend, says Monica Mazzei, a partner in Buchalter’s San Francisco family law office.

“It’s totally changed the landscape,” said Mazzei. “I’ve never seen this before. This was definitely big news in the family law space.”

Since the Nvidia scandal broke, three clients have contacted Mazzei with requests to draft NDAs for the significant others of CEOs. They specifically cited Huang in the outreach, said Mazzei, who specializes in representing high-net-worth clients. Most of the requests are coming from the company, not the CEO themselves, in an effort to protect the business.

“The company is probably telling the CEO, ‘Anyone you need to date needs to sign this because we don’t want you to end up in a Jensen Huang situation,’” Mazzei said.

Huang had at least three known affairs, two with internal Nvidia employees, and one extra controversial relationship with Alice Huang (no relation), an executive at the Singapore-based company Megaspeed. Alice Huang is reportedly suspected by some intelligence officials of being a Chinese spy and of illegally providing Chinese companies access to advanced Nvidia chips. The allegations are that Alice Huang is a “honeypot” who lured Jensen Huang into a relationship to get access to proprietary information.

“Why honeypots work is because when you’re dating someone you’re not thinking about what they might overhear on a phone call, or see on papers lying out at home,” said Mazzei. “They’re just in your life, overhearing a lot.”

Demand for prenuptial agreements has also surged. Jensen and Lori Huang have been married for 41 years, and reportedly do not have a prenuptial agreement. Jensen Huang is one of the richest people in the world, with a net worth of roughly $137 billion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. According to California law, Lori stands to come away with half of that in a potential divorce, along with shares in Nvidia.

It remains to be seen if Lori Huang will file for a divorce. If the couple were to decide to split up, Lori and Jensen Huang would most likely agree to a settlement prior to the divorce proceedings becoming public, says Mazzei. Once the terms are finalized, Mazzei reckons, the couple would then go public with the news, as Jeff Bezos and Mackenzie Scott did.

Libby Leffler, founder and CEO of thisfirst.com, an online prenup service, says she’s seen more customers naming tech billionaires and founders as the inspiration for their agreements since the Nvidia scandal broke. Most of Leffler’s clients are founders and early employees at pre-IPO companies, especially in California and New York. Every time a public figure’s divorce or prenup makes headlines, Leffler’s inbound requests jump, but the naming of tech CEOs this time is different.

“People used to name-check celebs, but now they are name-checking tech CEOs,” Leffler tells Fortune. “What they really mean is that they want to feel as protected as they assume those people are.” The most referenced arrangement is Jeff Bezos’s rumored prenuptial agreement with Lauren Sánchez, who became his second wife in 2025.

“Your relationship and your cap table are more connected than people think, and founders are seeing that play out,” Leffler said.

Mazzei also noted a surge in prenup requests, specifically coming from Anthropic employees. When the company went public at a $1.5 trillion valuation on Nov. 19—a week after Huang’s ousting—it minted thousands of multimillionaires among the company’s relatively small staff of 5,300. The average fortune of its non-founding staff is roughly $44 million, although nearly 600 pocketed at least $100 million.

Mazzei could not link the Anthropic employees’ requests to Nvidia directly, although the Huangs’ lack of a prenup may have spooked them. In general, many of them are on the younger side, and Mazzei noted that among younger generations prenups are becoming more common.

#5322. Grand Theft Auto VI Made $3.79 Billion In One Day. Taylor Swift’s Entire Eras Tour Made About Half That.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Rockstar is calling its new release the biggest entertainment launch in history — and the numbers are highway robbery.

Taylor Swift spent 21 months on the road to gross roughly $2 billion with the Eras Tour, a music industry record. Then Grand Theft Auto VI rolled into town and nearly doubled that in a single day, PEOPLE reports.

Rockstar Games and parent company Take-Two Interactive say GTA VI sales reached $3.79 billion worldwide on its release date. That’s based on company estimates. Rockstar calls it “the biggest entertainment launch in history” in a press release. The game also sold a record 32.5 million units before it even came out. (It costs $79.99 for the Standard Edition and $99.99 for the Ultimate Edition.)

For context, the previous installment, GTA V, debuted in 2013 and made $815.7 million in its first 24 hours. That mark previously held the Guinness World Record for the most a video game has earned in a day.

GTA VI has a long way to travel to catch its predecessor, though. Take-Two says GTA V has sold nearly 235 million units.

#5321. 8 of the biggest MLB contracts for Japanese players, from $700 million to $34 million

Eight of the largest MLB deals for Japanese players, from Ohtani's $700 million to Murakami's $34 million, and what each total leaves out.

Major league teams now compete to sign the best players from Nippon Professional Baseball, Japan's top league, and fans tend to judge each of those signings by the total written on the contract. That total leaves out a second payment, because a team that signs a posted Japanese star pays the player and also pays the Japanese club that let him go. MLB.com reports that the Yankees paid Masahiro Tanaka's Japanese club a posting fee separate from his contract. The Blue Jays owed the same kind of fee to Kazuma Okamoto's club under MLB's agreement with NPB, with that money kept outside his contract, according to CBC. The second bill is a standing part of the price of Japanese talent. It keeps rising on deals past $50 million, with the Japanese club taking 15% of any value above that mark, according to CBS Sports. None of that money appears in the headline figure, so the total fans quote covers only part of what a team spends.

Deadlines also shape the price, and they favor the team most willing to spend. Once his club posts him, a Japanese player has 45 days to negotiate with MLB teams, according to MLB.com. Every interested team has to make its best offer within the same few weeks. The final number reflects how many teams wanted the player and how badly they needed him, as much as his record in Japan. The years and dollars on paper can also differ from what a team actually pays and how long the player stays. Money deferred for years costs a team less than money paid now, and an opt-out can end a deal well before its last season. Fans who compare totals learn less than it seems about who is the better player, and the smallest deal can turn out to be the best one.

ESPN set out to rank the largest MLB deals that Japanese players have signed, including the Yankees' 2014 contract for Masahiro Tanaka, the Cubs' deal for Teruaki Sato and the White Sox's deal for Munetaka Murakami. Each of those totals is the money a team promised, and it is best read as a starting point. Behind a total can sit a fee owed to a club in Japan, pay that arrives years later, an exit the player controls or a team in a hurry to fill a hole. Read that way, the order of these deals says more about what each team promised than about what each player turned out to be worth.

Shohei Ohtani signed the richest contract a Japanese player has ever received, and the Dodgers paid it for a star they had already watched in the majors. Los Angeles committed $700 million over 10 years to a player who had spent six seasons across town with the Angels, according to ESPN. Nobody had to guess whether his game would carry over from Japan, so the hard question about the deal is how the Dodgers built it. The Associated Press reports that 97% of the money was deferred without interest when he signed in 2023. Almost all of the record total is a promise to pay later, and the question that matters is when the Dodgers actually hand the money over.

The Dodgers will pay most of Ohtani's money long after he signed, and they will spread it across a decade. The deferred payments arrive each July 1 from 2034 through 2043, according to The Associated Press. A dollar paid that far in the future, with no interest added, is worth less than a dollar paid today, and the Dodgers' real cost is below $700 million. Nobody needs to settle on an exact figure for that gap to matter. Ohtani's total can't be compared directly with a contract that pays a player during the seasons he plays.

The 10 years are also less certain than they look, because Ohtani can leave for reasons that have nothing to do with how he plays. The Associated Press reports that the 2023 contract lets him opt out if Mark Walter stops being the controlling owner or if Andrew Friedman leaves as president of baseball operations. A change in the front office, rather than a slump, could end the decade early.

The record contract puts off most of its payments for a decade and leaves its length in the hands of the team's owner and its top baseball executive.

The Dodgers committed more money to Yoshinobu Yamamoto than any team had committed to a player moving straight from Japan to the majors, and they did it before he had thrown a major league pitch. His $325 million contract is the largest for a player arriving directly from Japan, according to ESPN. The Los Angeles Times reports that he was 25 when he signed in 2023, and that before bidding opened, he was expected to command at least $200 million. Clubs judged him on his pitching in Japan, where he won the Pacific League's MVP award in three consecutive seasons. Teams kept raising their offers well past that early estimate, and his final price measures how hard clubs competed for him as much as how good he was.

The Dodgers bid the highest because signing Yamamoto served a plan built around Shohei Ohtani. Ohtani helped recruit him, taking part with teammates Betts and Freeman in the meeting the Dodgers held with Yamamoto at their ballpark, according to the Los Angeles Times. "It was important to Shohei that this wasn't the one move we were gonna make, and I think anyone who has watched us operate over the years, we're trying to add really good players at every turn," Andrew Friedman, the Dodgers' president of baseball operations, told the Los Angeles Times in 2023. A team that had made that promise to its biggest star had little reason to stop bidding at the early estimate. When several teams compete for one player, the team with the most pressing plan usually decides the final price.

So far, Yamamoto has pitched well enough to justify the Dodgers' spending. He earned the World Series MVP award in 2025, according to MLB.com. Paying well above the early estimate looks less like a mistake when the player is judged the most valuable performer in the World Series. The competition among teams raised what the Dodgers spent, but it did not make the deal a bad one.

The Dodgers paid extra to sign him, and so far he has pitched like the player they were bidding for.

The Yankees offered Masahiro Tanaka a sum that few pitchers of any background had received. New York signed him for $155 million over seven years in 2014, according to ESPN. MLB.com reports that it was then the fifth-highest contract ever given to a pitcher, and only Kershaw, Verlander, Hernandez and Sabathia had been paid more. The Yankees put a pitcher who came directly from Nippon Professional Baseball, and who had never thrown a major league inning, in the same pay bracket as those four.

New York spent more to get Tanaka than the figure that ranks him. The Yankees also paid Rakuten, the Japanese club that posted him, $20 million for the right to sign him, according to MLB.com. That payment bought permission alone, and none of it went to Tanaka. The Yankees' real bet on him was larger than his ranked total.

The Yankees made their case for Tanaka entirely on what he had done in Japan. In 2013, his last season with Rakuten, he went 24-0 with a 1.27 ERA, according to MLB.com. No team had seen him face major league hitters, so that season showed promise rather than proof. The Yankees still bid as if they would never get another chance. "That was our one shot, and we took it very seriously," Yankees general manager Brian Cashman said in 2014.

The Yankees paid to find out what Tanaka could do against major league hitters, not to buy a record he had already set there.

The Chicago Cubs paid one of the highest prices ever for a hitter coming from Japan, and they paid it for the best batting season any player there had put together in years. ESPN reports that Sato agreed to $120 million over six years with the Cubs, the third-largest deal for a player from Japan's league. Sato became the first Triple Crown winner in Japan since Munetaka Murakami's 2022 season, according to CBS Sports. The Cubs are paying for the one skill Sato showed best, his power. They are not paying for a hitter without flaws.

Sato misses the ball far more often than a typical major league hitter, and the Cubs signed him anyway. He made contact on 66% of his swings, against a major league average of 77%, according to CBS Sports. That gap means he will likely strike out more than most hitters once he faces major league pitching. Chicago is betting that his home runs will outweigh the empty swings, and the six-year term shows the team expects that power to last for years. "Like Murakami, Sato carries risk, and like Murakami, his power makes that risk worth the dice roll," CBS Sports writer Dayn Perry wrote.

The Cubs took that risk because the departure of two regulars left them short of a bat. Ian Happ and Seiya Suzuki both left in free agency, according to CBS Sports, and together they were worth 7.8 wins above a replacement player in 2026. Sato is being asked to replace a large share of that production by himself. Chicago plans to use him in left or right field, even though he is known mainly as a first or third baseman, and his biggest adjustment will be the better pitching he faces. Sato's price reflects how badly Chicago needed a bat as much as it reflects the quality of his bat.

Toronto turned to Kaima Taira after several other starting pitchers it pursued signed elsewhere. The Blue Jays agreed to pay him $80 million over five years, with a $5 million bonus and an opt-out, according to ESPN. Tarik Skubal chose the New York Mets even though Toronto had reportedly offered him nine years and $420 million, according to USA TODAY. Two more starters the team went after also landed with other clubs, with Trevor Rogers joining the Chicago Cubs and Freddy Peralta joining the Baltimore Orioles. MLB's labor deal expires Dec. 1, and Toronto chose to fill its rotation before that deadline rather than keep searching. The team paid Taira's price out of need and failed pursuits as much as for anything he did on the mound.

Toronto is paying mostly for Taira's return to starting. After working strictly in relief as a closer in 2025, he moved back into a rotation in 2026 and led every qualified starter in Japan with a 1.36 ERA, according to USA TODAY. He has never thrown more than 150 innings in a season, yet Toronto will likely slot him third in its rotation in 2027. The Blue Jays are betting less on the ERA than on whether his arm can last through a full season of starts.

The opt-out puts much of the reward in Taira's hands. If he holds up as a starter, he can leave and look for a better deal before the five years run out. If his arm wears down, the choice to stay is his as well, and Toronto keeps the cost.

Need brought Taira to Toronto, and his own success could take him away.

Toronto paid Kazuma Okamoto a solid price rather than a superstar's price. The Blue Jays gave him a four-year, $60 million contract, which tops the $54 million deal Tatsuya Imai signed, according to ESPN. Bringing him to Toronto cost the team more than his contract. Toronto must also send $10,875,000 to the Yomiuri Giants, the club he played for in Japan, according to CBC. A contender spent that much on a hitter who isn't a headline star because it needed a third baseman.

Toronto finished last season without a regular third baseman. Addison Barger and Ernie Clement split the starts at the position almost evenly, CBC reports, and neither player held the job. With this contract, the team bought a full-time answer at a position it had been filling day to day.

The Blue Jays are betting that Okamoto's power will carry over to the majors. He arrives directly from Japan's league with 248 career home runs, according to CBC, and he hit every one of them in Japan. Toronto paid for a proven record that major league pitching has yet to test. It did not pay for star power.

Okamoto settles one position in an infield that is otherwise uncertain. Bo Bichette is a free agent who has not re-signed, CBC reports, so Toronto may still have a hole elsewhere in the infield. The team put its largest money that winter into pitching. In the same winter it committed $60 million to Okamoto, Toronto gave Dylan Cease a seven-year, $210 million deal. That made Okamoto a supporting piece for a team spending heavily to win now.

Toronto paid Okamoto's price as a team in a hurry to fill a gap, and the figure is no measure of how good he will turn out to be.

Tatsuya Imai earned a place among the largest MLB contracts signed by Japanese players, though near the low end of that group, when the Astros gave him three years and $54 million, according to ESPN. Those three years look like a firm commitment from Houston. But Imai can opt out after the 2026 season, MLB.com reports, and he can opt out again after 2027, which means he could become a free agent after one or two seasons. The $54 million shows what the Astros promised him. How long he stays is Imai's decision.

Imai could take a short deal because his results have held up for years. He has posted a 2.18 ERA since 2023, according to MLB.com. That mark covers several seasons of work, so his success does not rest on a single strong year. His camp put him on the same level as Yoshinobu Yamamoto. "Certainly, he's done everything that Yamamoto's done in NPB," Scott Boras, Imai's agent, said. Even with that standing, Imai signed for three years instead of locking in his prime at a fixed rate. He kept the right to ask for a new price soon. The short term reads as Imai's wager on himself rather than a sign that teams doubted him.

The Astros accepted a deal that could end early because they needed starting pitchers right away. Three Astros pitchers had Tommy John surgery in 2025, according to MLB.com. Pitchers usually miss more than a season after that operation, so the Astros faced the coming year with holes in their rotation. They also expect to lose Framber Valdez, a mainstay of that rotation, in free agency. A team that short of starters now gains more from one or two excellent seasons than from waiting for a longer commitment.

The Astros are guaranteed to pay Imai $54 million, but they carry the risk that his success will take him to another team before the three years are up.

The White Sox may have paid too little for Munetaka Murakami rather than too much. Chicago signed him to a two-year, $34 million contract, according to ESPN, the smallest of the biggest deals Japanese players have signed with MLB teams. For that price, the team got power that only one other Japanese-born hitter has shown in the majors. Murakami and Shohei Ohtani are the only Japanese-born players with 35 or more home runs in a season, according to the Chicago Sun-Times. Murakami's contract is the smallest in this group, but his power puts him in the same company as the most celebrated Japanese hitter in the game.

Chicago has already received a full slugger's season from the first year of a short deal. By Sept. 25 of his rookie season, Murakami had hit 35 home runs, the Chicago Sun-Times reports, and only Jose Abreu and Ron Kittle had reached that mark as White Sox rookies. Murakami does most of his damage by pulling the ball toward right field, but 29% of his home runs have gone to center field or the left side. His power reaches more than one part of the park. One season of that production already makes a $34 million price look low.

Murakami came to Chicago straight from Japan's Nippon Professional Baseball, and one season later he is an important hitter for a White Sox team chasing the Cleveland Guardians in the AL Central. His value is being tested in games that matter now, and the bargain depends on him staying at this level. "We know how impactful he can be when he's right and feeling good," White Sox manager Will Venable said, as reported by the Chicago Sun-Times. Chicago signed Murakami for only two seasons, and half of that time is nearly over. One poor season could erase the bargain.

Chicago got a historic return in the first year of the smallest of these deals, and only Murakami's second season can show whether he can repeat it.
